source: Written 2026-10-17 by Claude Sonnet and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin. Hand-written fixture questions are "approved".

notes.NC26.6.RPR.2: No figures: double number lines are described by their paired marks in the question, and graphs by points written as (x, y) with what each coordinate means. Percent answers in choice questions keep the % sign (checked by direct calculation in the build script); numeric percent answers ask "what percent" and are given without the sign. Conversion factors that are not obvious (pints, ounces, grams) are stated in the question. No percent over 100, no percent increase/decrease or sale-price questions (later grades); the harder percent items are multi-step uses of part, whole and percent only.
notes.NC26.6.ANR.2: Written fresh: 90 questions (30 per difficulty) across thirteen skills. No figures or models are used; "dividing with models" is tested through how-many-fit and sharing stories and by choosing the expression a story needs. Answers may be given as a mixed number, an improper fraction or a decimal.
notes.NC26.6.ANR.5: Number lines are described in words (marks counted from 0), never drawn. Choice answers that are fractions, mixed numbers, statements or lists have no compute; decimal and integer choice answers do. Fractions have denominators up to 20; decimals go to thousandths. The fraction/decimal-valued numeric answers are given as decimals or a/b.
notes.NC26.6.ANR.7: Equations use non-negative numbers only (whole numbers, decimals and fractions). Number-line graphs are described in words (open or closed circle, direction of the arrow), never drawn. Options that are equations or inequalities were checked by substitution in the script.
notes.NC26.6.SGMR.2: All questions are text only: every point or polygon is given as coordinates written in the stem. Distances and side lengths are only ever along horizontal or vertical lines; the one slanted side (a 3-4-5 triangle) has its length stated. Quadrant numbering is explained in each stem that names a quadrant by number.
notes.NC26.6.SGMR.3: No figures: every net is described by its faces (for example "2 hexagons and 6 rectangles"), and every solid by its measurements. Triangular-prism and pyramid problems give every length the surface area needs (triangle base, height and sides; faces of a pyramid with their own base and height). Volume of a triangular prism is not asked (a later grade). Answers that need a square root (a cube from its surface area, a square base from its volume) use whole-number results, so they carry no compute string.
notes.NC26.6.RD.3: No figures: every dot plot, line plot, histogram and box plot is written out as stacks, bars or five key values. Quartiles are the medians of the lower and upper halves (the median is left out when the number of values is odd, and the stem says so); wherever the data have an even count the choice of method does not matter. Several items test what a histogram or box plot can and cannot show (smallest/greatest possible range, median position, the share of data in each quarter). Non-standard displays are a line plot with fractions, a box plot standing up, a number line with ticks between labels, decimals on a line plot and a histogram scaled in percents.
notes.NC26.6.RD.4: No figures: every data set is written out. "Comparing displays" is covered by comparing two written-out data sets (range, IQR, same mean with different spread). IQR (quartiles as medians of the lower and upper halves, middle value left out for an odd count) is defined in the stem each time it is used. Data are non-negative; decimals appear only where the standard sums to a terminating decimal.
notes.NC26.6.ANR.1: No figures needed. Factor trees are described in words (the splits are stated), and lists of factors or multiples are given only where the question asks to read them. Least common multiples mostly use numbers up to 12 (a few in context go to 15 or 20, and one context item uses three numbers); greatest common factors use numbers up to 108. Choice items whose answers are exponent expressions or sums keep LaTeX options, so they have no compute (the build script checks their values by calculation). A few difficulty-3 items are reverse questions (find the number from its GCF or LCM) with a unique answer checked by enumeration. No algebra with variables other than a blank or a letter standing for a single missing whole number.
notes.NC26.6.ANR.3: Written fresh: 90 questions (30 per difficulty) across ten skills. Quotients are all terminating decimals; factors and divisors are to the hundredths. Money is written in words.
notes.NC26.6.ANR.4: Operands and answers stay within -20 to 20 (a few intermediate steps in difficulty-3 sign-reasoning items, and the chip counts, go slightly past it). Chip and number-line models are described in words, with no figures. Choice answers that are statements or expressions have no compute.
notes.NC26.6.ANR.6: Whole-number bases and exponents only; fraction and decimal values appear just in evaluation (a cube of edge 1/2 foot, 3/4 m + 5). Sets of options that are algebraic expressions were checked by evaluating every option at several values; numeric keys by exact computation.
notes.NC26.6.RD.1: No figures: every spinner is described by its sections, every bag by its contents, and the one table of results is written out in the question. Every random pick says "at random" or "without looking" and every die, coin and spinner is fair or has equal sections. Numeric probabilities are fractions or decimals (any equivalent form is accepted); the few percent answers say to give the number without the percent sign. Questions about dice use only a single roll, a single pick or a single spin (no two-step events).
notes.NC26.6.RD.2: No figures: every list, tally and table is written out in the question. Statistical-question, bias and sampling items are choice questions or counts ("how many of the questions are ...") with clear-cut cases only; borderline questions (a single count of people at one moment) are avoided as keys. Fractions of the population, percents and proportional shares use grade-6 numbers. The proportional-sample items (shares by grade) are on the stretch end of the standard.
notes.NC26.6.RD.5: No figures: every data set, tally and rating scale is written out in the question. Conclusions, bias and sampling items are choice questions with clear-cut cases (random draw versus convenience sample, leading wording, one class versus a whole state); the items that ask for a number use percents, fractions of a population, counts and medians from written-out data. IQR items (about 4 of 90) define the quartiles in the stem each time (median of the lower and upper halves, middle value left out for an odd count). No dependence on the words skewed, symmetric or mean absolute deviation.
notes.NC26.6.RPR.1: Ratios are written as $a : b$, "a to b" and the fraction $\frac{a}{b}$. A ratio is never itself the answer to a numeric question, so numeric questions ask for a number inside a ratio (the missing value n, a count, a unit ratio) or for a ratio written as a fraction (accepted in any equivalent form). Ratio-valued answers are choice questions. Ten skills, 9 questions each (3 at each difficulty). Three-quantity ratios (R10) and ratio tables are used lightly, only to test ratio language and equivalent ratios. Unit-ratio questions use whole numbers, decimals and simple fractions; all unit ratios are "per 1" of the second quantity or the first, never rates with units to convert. No dollar signs: money is written in words.
notes.NC26.6.SGMR.1: Numbers are mostly whole; decimals only where the standard works with them (A, B, D). Trapezoid area is asked through half of (sum of parallel sides) times height or through two copies making a parallelogram. Rhombus is treated as a parallelogram. No figures are referred to; every shape is described by its measurements.

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: A bag has 5 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. What is the ratio of red marbles to blue marbles?
questions.solution: "Red to blue" puts red first and blue second, so the ratio is 5 to 3. The ratio 3 to 5 is in the wrong order, and 5 to 8 and 3 to 8 compare one color to all 8 marbles.

solve.work: Red to blue is 5 to 3, in the order named.

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: A class has 9 girls and 11 boys. What is the ratio of girls to all of the students in the class?
questions.solution: There are 9 + 11 = 20 students in all. Girls to all students is 9 to 20. The ratio 9 to 11 compares girls to boys, not to all students.

solve.work: Total students = 9 + 11 = 20. Girls to all students = 9 to 20.

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios
questions.stem: The ratios $2 : 5$ and $6 : n$ are equivalent. What is the value of $n$?
questions.solution: To go from 2 to 6, multiply by 3. Multiply the 5 by 3 as well: $5 \times 3 = 15$. So $n = 15$.

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: A drawer has 8 black socks and 6 white socks. What is the ratio of white socks to black socks?
questions.solution: The ratio of white socks to black socks puts the white socks first: $6 : 8$. ($8 : 6$ has the order reversed, and $6 : 14$ and $8 : 14$ compare one color to all the socks.)

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: At a pet store, the ratio of puppies to kittens is 7 to 4. For every 7 puppies, how many kittens are there?
questions.solution: The ratio 7 to 4 means 4 kittens for every 7 puppies.

solve.work: 7 to 4 means 4 kittens for every 7 puppies.

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: Which sentence matches the ratio $3 : 5$ of pencils to pens?
choices: For every 3 pencils there are 5 pens
For every 5 pencils there are 3 pens
For every 3 pencils there are 8 pens
There are 3 more pens than pencils
questions.answer: For every 3 pencils there are 5 pens
questions.solution: In the ratio of pencils to pens, the 3 goes with pencils and the 5 goes with pens: 3 pencils for every 5 pens.

solve.answer: For every 3 pencils there are 5 pens
solve.work: Pencils to pens 3 : 5 -> for every 3 pencils there are 5 pens.

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: Of the 20 questions on a quiz, Sam answered 17 correctly. What is the ratio of correct answers to all of the questions?
questions.solution: The whole is all 20 questions, so the ratio of correct answers to all the questions is $17 : 20$. ($17 : 3$ compares correct to incorrect answers, and $20 : 17$ has the order reversed.)

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: A fruit basket holds 3 apples, 4 pears and 5 plums. The ratio of pears to all the fruit is 4 to what number?
questions.solution: The whole is all the fruit: $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ pieces. So the ratio of pears to all the fruit is 4 to 12.

solve.work: Total fruit 3 + 4 + 5 = 12; pears to all = 4 to 12.

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: Which sentence describes the ratio $5 : 12$ of girls to all students?
questions.solution: A part-to-whole ratio of $5 : 12$ means 5 out of every 12 students are girls. The 12 counts all the students, boys and girls together.

solve.work: Girls to all students 5 : 12 -> 5 of every 12 students are girls.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is $2 : 3$. Every member of the club is a boy or a girl. What is the ratio of boys to all the students in the club?
questions.solution: For every 2 boys there are 3 girls, so for every 2 boys there are $2 + 3 = 5$ students in all. The ratio of boys to all students is $2 : 5$.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: All the beads in a box are red or blue, and the ratio of red beads to blue beads is 1 to 2. The ratio of red beads to all the beads is 1 to what number?
questions.solution: For every 1 red bead there are 2 blue beads, so there are $1 + 2 = 3$ beads in all. The ratio of red to all is 1 to 3.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: In a garden, the ratio of tulips to daisies is $3 : 4$. All the flowers are tulips or daisies. What is the ratio of daisies to all the flowers?
questions.solution: For every 3 tulips there are 4 daisies, so there are $3 + 4 = 7$ flowers in all. The ratio of daisies to all the flowers is $4 : 7$.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: Which is another way to write the ratio $3 : 7$?
questions.solution: The ratio $3 : 7$ can also be read "3 to 7" or written as the fraction $\frac{3}{7}$. The other choices reverse the order or compare 3 to the total, 10.

solve.work: 3 : 7 = 3 to 7 = 3/7. 7/3 and 7 to 3 are reversed; 3 out of 10 is part to whole.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: The ratio of pens to markers is 2 to 5. Write this ratio as a fraction with the number of pens on top.
questions.solution: The first number is the top of the fraction and the second is the bottom, so 2 to 5 is the fraction $\frac{2}{5}$.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: A class has 12 boys and 10 girls. Which fraction shows the ratio of girls to boys?
questions.solution: Girls to boys is $10 : 12$, so the fraction has 10 on top and 12 on the bottom. ($\frac{10}{22}$ compares the girls to all the students.)

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 4 cups of milk. How many cups of milk are needed for 9 cups of flour?
questions.solution: 9 cups of flour is $9 \div 3 = 3$ times as much as 3 cups, so use 3 times as much milk: $3 \times 4 = 12$ cups.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: The ratio of bags to apples is 1 to 6. At the same ratio, how many apples are in 5 bags?
questions.solution: Each bag has 6 apples, so 5 bags have $5 \times 6 = 30$ apples.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: A paint mix uses 2 cans of blue paint for every 5 cans of white paint. How many cans of blue paint go with 15 cans of white paint?
questions.solution: 15 cans of white is $15 \div 5 = 3$ groups of 5. Each group goes with 2 cans of blue, so $3 \times 2 = 6$ cans of blue.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Which ratio is equivalent to $1 : 3$?
questions.solution: Multiply both numbers of $1 : 3$ by 2 to get $2 : 6$. Adding 1 to both numbers gives $2 : 4$, which is not equivalent.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Sam makes lemonade with 2 lemons for every 4 cups of water. Which mix uses the same ratio of lemons to water?
questions.solution: 4 lemons and 8 cups doubles both amounts of 2 lemons and 4 cups, so the ratio stays the same. The other mixes do not multiply both amounts by the same number.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Which of these ratios is NOT equivalent to $3 : 4$?
questions.solution: $6 : 8$, $9 : 12$ and $12 : 16$ come from multiplying 3 and 4 by 2, 3 and 4. $5 : 6$ does not match any multiple of $3 : 4$.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: A class has 6 boys and 9 girls. What is the ratio of boys to girls in lowest terms?
questions.solution: Divide both 6 and 9 by 3 to get $2 : 3$. ($3 : 2$ reverses the order, and $2 : 5$ would compare the boys to all the students.)

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: A bag has 4 red marbles and 12 blue marbles. The ratio of red marbles to blue marbles in lowest terms is 1 to n. What is n?
questions.solution: Divide both numbers by 4: $4 : 12$ becomes $1 : 3$. So $n = 3$.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: Which ratio is written in lowest terms?
questions.solution: 3 and 5 have no common factor other than 1, so $3 : 5$ cannot be simplified. $4 : 6$ is $2 : 3$, $5 : 10$ is $1 : 2$ and $6 : 9$ is $2 : 3$.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: A pack of 6 pencils costs 12 dollars. How many dollars does 1 pencil cost?
questions.solution: Divide the cost by the number of pencils: $12 \div 6 = 2$ dollars for 1 pencil.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: Mia walks 8 miles in 2 hours at a steady pace. How many miles does she walk in 1 hour?
questions.solution: Divide the distance by the time: $8 \div 2 = 4$ miles in 1 hour.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: A machine fills 30 bottles in 5 minutes. How many bottles does it fill in 1 minute?
questions.solution: Divide: $30 \div 5 = 6$ bottles in 1 minute. (25 subtracts, 150 multiplies and 35 adds.)

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: A box holds 8 bags that have 24 apples in all, the same number in every bag. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: Divide the apples among the bags: $24 \div 8 = 3$ apples in 1 bag. (16 subtracts and 32 adds.)

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: Water flows from a tap at 3 liters per minute. How many minutes does it take to fill 1 liter? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: In 1 minute, 3 liters flow. So 1 liter takes $1 \div 3 = \frac{1}{3}$ of a minute.

solve.work: 3 liters per 1 minute -> 1 liter per 1/3 minute.

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: A bus travels 40 miles in 1 hour. What is the other unit ratio for this bus?
questions.solution: One unit ratio is 40 miles per 1 hour. The other is the time for 1 mile: $1 \div 40 = \frac{1}{40}$ hour for every 1 mile.

solve.work: 40 miles : 1 hour -> 1 mile : 1/40 hour, i.e. 1/40 hour for every 1 mile.

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: A bag has 2 red, 3 blue and 5 green marbles. What is the ratio of blue marbles to green marbles?
questions.solution: Blue marbles first, then green: $3 : 5$. ($3 : 10$ compares blue to all the marbles, and $5 : 3$ has the order reversed.)

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: A box has 6 red pens, 4 black pens and 2 blue pens. For every 1 blue pen, how many red pens are there?
questions.solution: There are 6 red pens for 2 blue pens. Divide both by 2: 3 red pens for 1 blue pen.

solve.work: Red to blue 6 : 2 = 3 : 1. 3 red per blue.

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: A jar has 5 pennies, 3 nickels and 2 dimes. Which statement is true?
choices: The ratio of nickels to all the coins is 3 to 7
The ratio of dimes to pennies is 5 to 2
The ratio of pennies to dimes is 2 to 5
The ratio of nickels to all the coins is 3 to 10
questions.answer: The ratio of nickels to all the coins is 3 to 10
questions.solution: All the coins: $5 + 3 + 2 = 10$, so nickels to all the coins is 3 to 10. Dimes to pennies is 2 to 5, and pennies to dimes is 5 to 2, so the other statements have the order reversed or leave out some coins.

solve.answer: The ratio of nickels to all the coins is 3 to 10
solve.work: Total 10. Nickels to all 3 to 10 (true). 3 to 7 false; dimes to pennies is 2 to 5, pennies to dimes 5 to 2, so B and C reversed.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: A car uses 6 gallons of gas to travel 150 miles. How many miles does the car travel on 1 gallon of gas?
questions.solution: Divide the miles by the gallons: $150 \div 6 = 25$. The car travels 25 miles on 1 gallon.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio as a fraction
questions.stem: A fruit bowl has 3 pears and 5 apples. Which fraction shows the ratio of pears to apples?
questions.solution: The ratio of pears to apples is 3 to 5, which is written $\frac{3}{5}$ with pears on top. $\frac{5}{3}$ has the order reversed, and $\frac{3}{8}$ and $\frac{5}{8}$ compare one fruit to all 8 pieces of fruit.

questions.skill: Recognizing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Which ratio is equivalent to $12 : 18$?
questions.solution: Divide both numbers by 6: $12 \div 6 = 2$ and $18 \div 6 = 3$, giving $2 : 3$. Subtracting 6 from each number (6 : 12) or adding 1 to each (13 : 19) does not keep the ratio equivalent, and 3 : 2 is in the wrong order.

solve.work: 12:18, divide both by 6: 2:3. 6:12 = 1:2 (no); 3:2 is reversed; 13:19 adds 1 (not equivalent).

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: On a team, the ratio of fifth graders to sixth graders is $4 : 3$. Which statement must be true?
choices: There are exactly 4 fifth graders and exactly 3 sixth graders on the team
There are 7 players on the team
For every 4 fifth graders there are 3 sixth graders
There are more sixth graders than fifth graders
questions.answer: For every 4 fifth graders there are 3 sixth graders
questions.solution: A ratio compares the amounts: 4 fifth graders for every 3 sixth graders. The team could be 8 and 6, or 12 and 9, so the exact numbers and the total are not known. There are more fifth graders than sixth graders.

solve.answer: For every 4 fifth graders there are 3 sixth graders
solve.work: A ratio gives relative amounts only: for every 4 fifth graders, 3 sixth graders. Totals need not be 7; there are more fifth graders.

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: A class has 15 girls. The ratio of girls to boys is 5 to 4. How many boys are in the class?
questions.solution: 15 girls is $15 \div 5 = 3$ groups of 5 girls. Each group has 4 boys, so there are $3 \times 4 = 12$ boys.

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: A park has 9 dogs and 6 cats. Which statement correctly uses ratio language?
choices: The ratio of cats to dogs is 9 to 6
The ratio of dogs to all animals is 9 to 6
The ratio of dogs to cats is 6 to 9
The ratio of dogs to cats is 9 to 6
questions.answer: The ratio of dogs to cats is 9 to 6
questions.solution: The first number goes with the animal named first. Dogs to cats is 9 to 6. Cats to dogs would be 6 to 9, and dogs to all the animals would be 9 to 15.

solve.answer: The ratio of dogs to cats is 9 to 6
solve.work: Dogs to cats = 9 to 6. Cats to dogs would be 6 to 9; dogs to all is 9 to 15.

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: A bag has 6 green marbles, 9 yellow marbles and 5 red marbles. What is the ratio of yellow marbles to all the marbles?
questions.solution: All the marbles: $6 + 9 + 5 = 20$. The ratio of yellow to all is $9 : 20$. ($9 : 11$ compares yellow to the marbles that are not yellow, and $9 : 14$ leaves out the green marbles.)

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: A school band has 30 members and 12 of them play brass instruments. Write the ratio of brass players to all the members as a fraction.
questions.solution: The ratio of brass players to all members is $12 : 30$, which is the fraction $\frac{12}{30}$. In lowest terms, $\frac{12}{30} = \frac{2}{5}$.

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: The ratio of students who bring lunch to all students in a school is 3 to 5. The school has 200 students. How many students bring lunch?
questions.solution: Split the 200 students into groups of 5: $200 \div 5 = 40$ groups. Each group has 3 students who bring lunch, so $40 \times 3 = 120$ students.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: The animals at a vet are cats and dogs in the ratio 5 to 3. There are 40 animals in all. How many are cats?
questions.solution: Each group has $5 + 3 = 8$ animals. There are $40 \div 8 = 5$ groups. Each group has 5 cats, so there are $5 \times 5 = 25$ cats.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: The ratio of walkers to riders in a school is $4 : 11$. Every student either walks or rides. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: For every 4 walkers there are 11 riders, which makes $4 + 11 = 15$ students. So 4 of every 15 students are walkers. (11 of every 15 are riders.)

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: A shelf has fiction and nonfiction books in the ratio 7 to 5. There are 60 books in all. How many are nonfiction?
questions.solution: Each group has $7 + 5 = 12$ books. There are $60 \div 12 = 5$ groups. Each group has 5 nonfiction books, so there are $5 \times 5 = 25$ nonfiction books.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: Which of these does NOT show the ratio of 4 cups of rice to 9 cups of water?
questions.solution: Rice is named first, so the 4 comes first: $4 : 9$, 4 to 9 and $\frac{4}{9}$ all show it. $9 : 4$ has the order reversed.

solve.work: Rice to water = 4 : 9 = 4 to 9 = 4/9. 9 : 4 is reversed.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: The ratio of wins to losses is written $\frac{9}{4}$. For every 4 losses, how many wins are there?
questions.solution: In the fraction, the top is the number of wins and the bottom is the number of losses. So there are 9 wins for every 4 losses.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: A bag has 5 red and 7 green marbles. Which shows the ratio of green marbles to all the marbles?
questions.solution: All the marbles: $5 + 7 = 12$. The green marbles come first, so the ratio is 7 to 12. (7 to 5 compares green to red.)

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls on a bus is 5 to 6. There are 30 boys on the bus. How many girls are on the bus?
questions.solution: 30 boys is $30 \div 5 = 6$ groups of 5. Each group has 6 girls, so there are $6 \times 6 = 36$ girls.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: A mixture uses 18 scoops of cocoa with 24 scoops of milk. At the same ratio, how many scoops of cocoa go with 4 scoops of milk?
questions.solution: Divide both amounts by 6: 18 scoops of cocoa and 24 scoops of milk become 3 scoops of cocoa and 4 scoops of milk. So 3 scoops of cocoa go with 4 scoops of milk.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: A train travels 150 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. How many miles does it travel in 5 hours?
questions.solution: In 1 hour the train travels $150 \div 3 = 50$ miles. In 5 hours it travels $5 \times 50 = 250$ miles.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: How many of these ratios are equivalent to $2 : 3$? $4 : 6$, $6 : 9$, $8 : 10$, $10 : 15$, $12 : 16$
questions.solution: $4 : 6$ (times 2), $6 : 9$ (times 3) and $10 : 15$ (times 5) are equivalent to $2 : 3$. $8 : 10$ is $4 : 5$ and $12 : 16$ is $3 : 4$ in lowest terms. So 3 ratios are equivalent.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Tess says $5 : 7$ and $10 : 12$ are equivalent because both numbers went up by 5. Which statement is true?
choices: They are not equivalent, because the second ratio was made by adding, not multiplying
They are equivalent, because both numbers went up by the same amount
They are equivalent, because the difference between the numbers is 2 in both
They are not equivalent, because $10 : 12$ is not a ratio
questions.answer: They are not equivalent, because the second ratio was made by adding, not multiplying
questions.solution: Equivalent ratios come from multiplying (or dividing) both numbers by the same number. Adding 5 to both does not keep the ratio: $5 : 7$ is not equal to $10 : 12$, since multiplying 5 by 2 gives 10 but 7 times 2 is 14.

solve.answer: They are not equivalent, because the second ratio was made by adding, not multiplying
solve.work: 5/7 is not 10/12 (=5/6). Adding the same amount does not keep a ratio; multiplying does.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Which pair of ratios is equivalent?
questions.solution: $6 : 8$ and $9 : 12$ are both $3 : 4$ in lowest terms. The other pairs are not: $8 : 10$ is $4 : 5$, $12 : 20$ is $3 : 5$ and $3 : 5$ is already lowest.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: A pond has 18 ducks and 30 geese. The ratio of ducks to geese in lowest terms is 3 to n. What is n?
questions.solution: Divide both numbers by 6: $18 : 30$ becomes $3 : 5$. So $n = 5$.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: Write the ratio of 24 minutes to 40 minutes in lowest terms.
questions.solution: Both numbers can be divided by 8: $24 \div 8 = 3$ and $40 \div 8 = 5$. So the ratio is $3 : 5$. ($6 : 10$ and $12 : 20$ are equivalent but can still be simplified.)

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: A farm has 28 cows and 20 pigs. Write the ratio of cows to pigs as a fraction in lowest terms.
questions.solution: Cows to pigs is $28 : 20$. Divide both by 4 to get $7 : 5$, which is the fraction $\frac{7}{5}$.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: A 5-pound bag of rice costs 12 dollars. How many dollars does 1 pound of rice cost?
questions.solution: Divide the cost by the number of pounds: $12 \div 5 = 2.4$ dollars for 1 pound.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: A hose fills 45 liters in 6 minutes. How many liters does it fill in 1 minute?
questions.solution: Divide: $45 \div 6 = 7.5$ liters in 1 minute.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: Three notebooks cost 7.50 dollars in all. How many dollars does 1 notebook cost?
questions.solution: Divide the total cost by the number of notebooks: $7.50 \div 3 = 2.50$ dollars for 1 notebook. (4.5 subtracts 3, 10.5 adds 3 and 22.5 multiplies by 3.)

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: Pam buys 4 books for 20 dollars. How many books can she buy for 1 dollar? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Divide the number of books by the cost: $4 \div 20 = \frac{4}{20} = \frac{1}{5}$ book for 1 dollar.

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: A cyclist rides 18 miles in 3 hours. Which pair gives both unit ratios?
choices: 6 miles per 1 hour and 6 hours per 1 mile
$\frac{1}{6}$ mile per 1 hour and 6 hours per 1 mile
6 miles per 1 hour and $\frac{1}{6}$ hour per 1 mile
15 miles per 1 hour and $\frac{1}{15}$ hour per 1 mile
questions.answer: 6 miles per 1 hour and $\frac{1}{6}$ hour per 1 mile
questions.solution: Miles per hour: $18 \div 3 = 6$. Hours per mile: $3 \div 18 = \frac{1}{6}$. The cyclist rides 6 miles in 1 hour, so 1 mile takes $\frac{1}{6}$ hour.

solve.answer: 6 miles per 1 hour and $\frac{1}{6}$ hour per 1 mile
solve.work: 18 / 3 = 6 miles per hour; 3 / 18 = 1/6 hour per mile.

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: Dev paints 4 square meters in 6 minutes. How many minutes does it take him to paint 1 square meter?
questions.solution: Divide the time by the area: $6 \div 4 = 1.5$ minutes for 1 square meter.

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: In a school play, the ratio of actors to singers to dancers is $2 : 3 : 5$. There are 30 singers. How many dancers are there?
questions.solution: 30 singers is $30 \div 3 = 10$ groups of 3. Each group goes with 5 dancers, so there are $10 \times 5 = 50$ dancers.

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: A paint mix has blue, white and yellow paint in the ratio $3 : 2 : 1$. Which statement is true?
choices: There is twice as much blue as white
For every 1 part of yellow there are 3 parts of blue
Yellow is half of the mix
For every 1 part of yellow there are 2 parts of blue
questions.answer: For every 1 part of yellow there are 3 parts of blue
questions.solution: In the ratio $3 : 2 : 1$, blue is 3 parts when yellow is 1 part. Blue is $\frac{3}{2}$ times the white, not twice as much, and yellow is 1 part out of 6, not half.

solve.answer: For every 1 part of yellow there are 3 parts of blue
solve.work: Blue 3, white 2, yellow 1. A false (3 blue per yellow); yellow is 1/6, not half; blue is 1.5 times white, not twice; D true.

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: A bag of 24 beads has red, green and blue beads in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$. How many beads are blue?
questions.solution: One group has $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$ beads. There are $24 \div 6 = 4$ groups. Each group has 3 blue beads, so there are $4 \times 3 = 12$ blue beads.

questions.skill: The two unit ratios in words
questions.stem: A school trip has 24 students and 8 teachers. Which statement is true?
choices: There are 3 teachers for every 1 student.
There are 3 students for every 1 teacher.
There are 16 students for every 1 teacher.
There are 8 students for every 1 teacher.
questions.answer: There are 3 students for every 1 teacher.
questions.solution: Divide: $24 \div 8 = 3$, so there are 3 students for every 1 teacher. (Equivalently, there is $\frac{1}{3}$ of a teacher for every student.) Subtracting 24 - 8 = 16 or using the number of teachers, 8, does not give a unit ratio.

solve.answer: There are 3 students for every 1 teacher.
solve.work: 24 students / 8 teachers = 3 students per teacher. Others: 16 per teacher (wrong), 3 teachers per student (reversed), 8 per teacher (wrong).

questions.skill: Unit ratio that is a fraction
questions.stem: Mia reads 6 pages in 15 minutes at a steady pace. How many pages does she read in 1 minute?
questions.solution: Divide the pages by the minutes: $6 \div 15 = \frac{6}{15} = \frac{2}{5}$. She reads $\frac{2}{5}$ of a page in 1 minute.

questions.skill: Ratio language with three quantities
questions.stem: A garden has 6 roses, 4 tulips and 10 daisies. Which statement is true?
choices: The ratio of roses to tulips is 4 to 6.
The ratio of roses to all of the flowers is 6 to 14.
The ratio of daisies to roses is 6 to 10.
The ratio of tulips to all of the flowers is 4 to 20.
questions.answer: The ratio of tulips to all of the flowers is 4 to 20.
questions.solution: There are $6 + 4 + 10 = 20$ flowers in all, so tulips to all flowers is 4 to 20. The other statements are false: roses to tulips is 6 to 4, daisies to roses is 10 to 6, and roses to all flowers is 6 to 20.

solve.answer: The ratio of tulips to all of the flowers is 4 to 20.
solve.work: Total = 6 + 4 + 10 = 20. Roses:tulips = 6:4 (option says 4:6, false). Tulips:all = 4:20 (true). Daisies:roses = 10:6 (option says 6:10, false). Roses:all = 6:20 (option says 6:14, false).

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: The ratio of cats to dogs at a shelter is $5 : 2$. Which could be the number of cats and dogs at the shelter?
questions.solution: The numbers must be 5 and 2 each multiplied by the same number. $20 : 8$ comes from multiplying both by 4. The others are $5 : 3$, $7 : 4$ and $2 : 1$ in simplest form.

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: The ratio of adults to children at a picnic is 3 to 7. There are 21 children. How many adults are at the picnic?
questions.solution: 21 children is $21 \div 7 = 3$ groups of 7 children. Each group goes with 3 adults, so there are $3 \times 3 = 9$ adults.

questions.skill: Part-to-part ratio language
questions.stem: The ratio of Ana's stickers to Ben's stickers is $4 : 1$. Which statement must be true?
choices: Ana has 4 times as many stickers as Ben
Ana has 3 more stickers than Ben
Ben has 4 times as many stickers as Ana
questions.answer: Ana has 4 times as many stickers as Ben
questions.solution: The ratio $4 : 1$ means Ana has 4 stickers for every 1 that Ben has, so she has 4 times as many. The actual numbers could be 4 and 1, or 8 and 2, so the other statements need not be true.

solve.answer: Ana has 4 times as many stickers as Ben
solve.work: 4 : 1 means Ana has 4 times as many as Ben. Exact counts and the difference are not fixed.

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: Which box could have a ratio of red pencils to all of its pencils of $1 : 4$?
choices: 5 red pencils and 20 pencils that are not red
5 red pencils and 15 pencils that are not red
4 red pencils and 20 pencils that are not red
20 red pencils and 5 pencils that are not red
questions.answer: 5 red pencils and 15 pencils that are not red
questions.solution: 5 red and 15 not red make $5 + 15 = 20$ pencils in all, and $5 : 20 = 1 : 4$. The others give $5 : 25$, $4 : 24$ and $20 : 25$, which are not $1 : 4$. (Compare red to not-red and you get $1 : 4$ for the second box, but that is a part-to-part ratio.)

solve.answer: 5 red pencils and 15 pencils that are not red

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: In a bag of 36 marbles, the ratio of blue marbles to all the marbles is 5 to 12. How many marbles are NOT blue?
questions.solution: Split the 36 marbles into groups of 12: $36 \div 12 = 3$ groups. Each group has 5 blue marbles, so there are $3 \times 5 = 15$ blue marbles. The rest are not blue: $36 - 15 = 21$.

questions.skill: Part-to-whole ratio language
questions.stem: Ravi says, "A class has 8 boys and 12 girls, so the ratio of girls to all the students is $12 : 8$." What mistake did Ravi make?
choices: He wrote the number of girls first
He added the girls and boys to get 12
He should have compared boys to all the students
He compared girls to boys, not to all the students
questions.answer: He compared girls to boys, not to all the students
questions.solution: All the students are $8 + 12 = 20$, so the ratio of girls to all students is $12 : 20$. Ravi wrote $12 : 8$, which compares girls to boys. Putting the girls first was correct.

solve.answer: He compared girls to boys, not to all the students
solve.work: 12 : 8 is girls to boys; girls to all is 12 : 20.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: A jar has sweet and sour candies in the ratio 5 to 2. There are 42 candies in all. How many more sweet candies than sour candies are there?
questions.solution: Each group has $5 + 2 = 7$ candies, and there are $42 \div 7 = 6$ groups. That is $6 \times 5 = 30$ sweet and $6 \times 2 = 12$ sour candies. The difference is $30 - 12 = 18$.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: The ratio of apples to all the fruit in a bowl is $3 : 8$. What is the ratio of apples to the fruit that are not apples?
questions.solution: Of every 8 pieces of fruit, 3 are apples, so $8 - 3 = 5$ are not apples. The ratio of apples to the other fruit is $3 : 5$.

solve.work: Apples 3 of 8, others 5; apples to non-apples = 3 : 5.

questions.skill: Moving between part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios
questions.stem: In a school, the ratio of students who ride the bus to all students is 3 to 8. There are 160 students. How many students do NOT ride the bus?
questions.solution: Groups of 8 students: $160 \div 8 = 20$ groups. Each group has 3 bus riders, so there are $20 \times 3 = 60$ bus riders. The others: $160 - 60 = 100$ students.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: The ratio of pens to pencils is written $\frac{6}{4}$. Which statement is true?
choices: For every 6 pencils there are 4 pens
For every 6 pens there are 10 pencils
For every 4 pens there are 10 pencils
For every 6 pens there are 4 pencils
questions.answer: For every 6 pens there are 4 pencils
questions.solution: In the fraction, pens are on top and pencils are on the bottom, so there are 6 pens for every 4 pencils. The other statements reverse the order or add the 6 and 4 to get 10.

solve.answer: For every 6 pens there are 4 pencils
solve.work: Pens/pencils = 6/4: for every 6 pens there are 4 pencils.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: Dee writes the ratio of cats to dogs as $\frac{7}{3}$. How many dogs are there for every 14 cats?
questions.solution: The fraction $\frac{7}{3}$ means 7 cats for every 3 dogs. 14 cats is $14 \div 7 = 2$ groups of 7, so there are $2 \times 3 = 6$ dogs.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in different notations
questions.stem: The ratio of blue tiles to red tiles is 5 to 8. Which pair shows this ratio in two different ways?
questions.solution: Blue is first, so the ratio is $5 : 8$, which can also be written $\frac{5}{8}$ or "5 to 8". The other pairs reverse the order in one of the two ways or use 13, the total number of tiles.

solve.work: Blue to red 5 to 8 = 5 : 8 = 5/8. Others reverse or use the total.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: A ratio table has the columns $4 : 10$, $6 : 15$ and $10 : n$. What is $n$?
questions.solution: The columns $4 : 10$ and $6 : 15$ both equal $2 : 5$. For the first number to be 10, multiply $2 : 5$ by 5 to get $10 : 25$. So $n = 25$.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: A school has 3 teachers for every 48 students. At the same ratio, how many teachers does a school with 336 students need?
questions.solution: 336 students is $336 \div 48 = 7$ groups of 48 students. Each group has 3 teachers, so the school needs $7 \times 3 = 21$ teachers.

questions.skill: Finding a missing value in equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Which value of $n$ makes $8 : 12 = n : 15$ true?
questions.solution: The ratio $8 : 12$ is $2 : 3$ in lowest terms. For the second number to be 15, multiply by 5: $2 \times 5 = 10$ and $3 \times 5 = 15$. So $n = 10$. (11 comes from adding 3 to both numbers, which does not keep the ratio.)

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Three recipes use oats and raisins. Recipe A uses 4 cups of oats and 6 cups of raisins. Recipe B uses 6 cups of oats and 9 cups of raisins. Recipe C uses 10 cups of oats and 14 cups of raisins. Which recipes use the same ratio of oats to raisins?
questions.solution: Recipe A is $4 : 6 = 2 : 3$ and Recipe B is $6 : 9 = 2 : 3$, so they match. Recipe C is $10 : 14 = 5 : 7$, which is different.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: How many ratios equivalent to $2 : 3$ have whole numbers and a second number of 18 or less? Count $2 : 3$ itself.
questions.solution: The second number must be a multiple of 3 (the first is then the same multiple of 2): 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18. That gives $2 : 3$, $4 : 6$, $6 : 9$, $8 : 12$, $10 : 15$ and $12 : 18$, which is $18 \div 3 = 6$ ratios.

questions.skill: Recognizing and testing equivalent ratios
questions.stem: Which list shows ratios that are all equivalent to each other?
questions.solution: In the first list each ratio is $2 : 3$ times 1, 2, 3 and 4. The other lists add the same amount to both numbers, which does not keep the ratio.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: A class has 45 students and 18 of them are boys. What is the ratio of boys to all the students in lowest terms?
questions.solution: Boys to all students is $18 : 45$. Divide both by 9 to get $2 : 5$. ($2 : 3$ compares the boys to the girls, $3 : 5$ is girls to all students, and $5 : 2$ has the order reversed.)

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: The ratio $48 : 72$ is written in lowest terms as $a : b$. What is $a + b$?
questions.solution: Divide both numbers by 24: $48 : 72$ becomes $2 : 3$. So $a = 2$, $b = 3$ and $a + b = 5$.

questions.skill: Writing a ratio in lowest terms
questions.stem: Maya uses $1\frac{1}{2}$ cups of flour and 2 cups of sugar. Written with whole numbers in lowest terms, the ratio of flour to sugar is 3 to n. What is n?
questions.solution: Double both amounts to remove the fraction: $1\frac{1}{2} \times 2 = 3$ and $2 \times 2 = 4$. So the ratio is $3 : 4$ and $n = 4$.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: A runner goes $3\frac{1}{2}$ miles in 28 minutes at a steady pace. How many miles does the runner go in 1 minute? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Divide the distance by the time: $3\frac{1}{2} \div 28 = \frac{7}{2} \div 28 = \frac{7}{56} = \frac{1}{8}$ mile in 1 minute.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: Pete reads 45 pages in $1\frac{1}{2}$ hours at a steady pace. How many pages does he read in 1 hour?
questions.solution: In $\frac{1}{2}$ hour he reads $45 \div 3 = 15$ pages, since $1\frac{1}{2}$ hours is 3 half-hours. In 1 hour (2 half-hours) he reads $2 \times 15 = 30$ pages. Or $45 \div 1\frac{1}{2} = 30$.

questions.skill: Unit ratio (amount per 1)
questions.stem: A store sells 8 ounces of cheese for 3.20 dollars. How many dollars does 1 ounce of cheese cost?
questions.solution: Divide the cost by the number of ounces: $3.20 \div 8 = 0.40$ dollars, or 0.4, for 1 ounce.

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: A snail crawls 12 centimeters in 8 minutes. How many minutes does it take the snail to crawl 1 centimeter? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Divide the time by the distance: $8 \div 12 = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$ minute for 1 centimeter.

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: Ahmed mows 3 lawns in $2\frac{1}{4}$ hours. How many lawns does he mow in 1 hour? Write your answer as a fraction or mixed number.
questions.solution: Divide the lawns by the hours: $3 \div 2\frac{1}{4} = 3 \div \frac{9}{4} = 3 \times \frac{4}{9} = \frac{12}{9} = 1\frac{1}{3}$ lawns in 1 hour.

questions.skill: The two unit ratios of one relationship
questions.stem: Tom says, "A car that goes 50 miles on 2 gallons goes 25 miles per gallon and uses 25 gallons per mile." What did Tom get wrong?
choices: Gallons per mile should be $\frac{1}{25}$, not 25
questions.answer: Gallons per mile should be $\frac{1}{25}$, not 25
questions.solution: Miles per gallon: $50 \div 2 = 25$, which is right. Gallons per mile: $2 \div 50 = \frac{1}{25}$ gallon for every mile, not 25 gallons.

solve.answer: Gallons per mile should be $\frac{1}{25}$, not 25
solve.work: 50 / 2 = 25 miles per gallon is right; gallons per mile = 2/50 = 1/25, not 25.

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: A fruit salad has apples, grapes and berries in the ratio $4 : 3 : 5$. There are 36 pieces of fruit in all. How many pieces are berries?
questions.solution: One group has $4 + 3 + 5 = 12$ pieces. There are $36 \div 12 = 3$ groups. Each group has 5 berries, so there are $3 \times 5 = 15$ berries. (9 is the grapes and 12 is the apples.)

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: At a camp, the ratio of adults to boys to girls is $2 : 5 : 7$. There are 70 boys. How many people are at the camp in all?
questions.solution: 70 boys is $70 \div 5 = 14$ groups of 5. Each group has $2 + 5 + 7 = 14$ people, so the camp has $14 \times 14 = 196$ people.

solve.work: Boys 5 parts = 70, part = 14; total 14 parts x 14 = 196 (adults 28, girls 98).

questions.skill: Ratios of three quantities and totals
questions.stem: Red, blue and green marbles are in a bag in the ratio $1 : 3 : 4$. Which could be the total number of marbles?
questions.solution: Each group has $1 + 3 + 4 = 8$ marbles, so the total must be a multiple of 8. Of the choices, only 40 is: $40 = 5 \times 8$.

solve.work: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8 parts; total must be a multiple of 8. Only 40.

questions.skill: Ratio table (scaling)
questions.stem: A recipe uses 2 cups of rice for every 3 cups of water. How many cups of water are needed for 10 cups of rice?
questions.solution: 10 cups of rice is $10 \div 2 = 5$ times as much as 2 cups, so multiply the water by 5: $3 \times 5 = 15$ cups.

solve.work: Rice:water = 2:3. 10 cups rice = 5 x 2, so water = 5 x 3 = 15.

questions.skill: Percent of a quantity
questions.stem: What is 25% of 80?
questions.solution: 25% means 25 per 100, or $\frac{25}{100} = \frac{1}{4}$. One fourth of 80 is $80 \div 4 = 20$.

questions.skill: Finding a percent
questions.stem: Sam answered 9 out of 10 questions correctly on a quiz. What percent of the questions did Sam answer correctly?
questions.solution: 9 out of 10 is the same rate as 90 out of 100, so Sam answered 90% of the questions correctly.

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table compares cups of flour to cups of sugar. The first row is 2 and 5. The second row has 6 cups of flour. How many cups of sugar are in the second row?
questions.solution: Flour went from 2 cups to 6 cups, which is 3 times as much. The sugar must be 3 times as much too: $5 \times 3 = 15$ cups.

solve.work: Flour:sugar = 2:5. 6 flour is 2 x 3, so sugar = 5 x 3 = 15.

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: One row of a ratio table shows the numbers 4 and 10. Which pair of numbers could be another row of the same ratio table?
questions.solution: Multiply both numbers by 2: $4 \times 2 = 8$ and $10 \times 2 = 20$. Adding the same number to both (8 and 14, or 6 and 12) or changing only one number (2 and 10) does not keep the ratio.

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table shows that Mia walks 2 miles in 40 minutes. At the same pace, how many miles does she walk in 120 minutes?
questions.solution: 120 minutes is 3 times as long as 40 minutes, so she walks 3 times as far: $2 \times 3 = 6$ miles.

solve.work: 120 min = 3 x 40 min, so miles = 3 x 2 = 6.

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: A fruit punch uses 1 cup of lemonade for every 4 cups of iced tea. How many cups of iced tea are needed to go with 5 cups of lemonade?
questions.solution: For each cup of lemonade there are 4 cups of tea. With 5 cups of lemonade, use $5 \times 4 = 20$ cups of iced tea.

solve.work: 1 lemonade : 4 tea. 5 lemonade -> 5 x 4 = 20 cups tea.

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is 2 to 3. Which could be the numbers of boys and girls in the club?
questions.solution: Doubling both parts of 2 to 3 gives 4 to 6, so 4 boys and 6 girls. Adding 1 to the girls (4 and 5) or adding 3 to both parts (5 and 6) does not keep the ratio, and 3 boys and 2 girls reverses it.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: On a double number line, the top marks 3, 6 and 9 are paired with the bottom marks 4, 8 and 12. What is the ratio of the top number to the bottom number, in simplest form?
questions.solution: Each pair, such as 3 and 4, has the top number first. Since 3 and 4 have no common factor, the ratio of top to bottom is 3 to 4. (4 to 3 is bottom to top.)

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: A double number line shows hours worked and dollars earned. The hours marks are 0, 2, 4 and 6, and the dollars marks directly below them are 0, 10, 20 and 30. If the number line is continued, how many dollars match 8 hours?
questions.solution: Each step of 2 hours adds 10 dollars. After 6 hours (30 dollars) the next mark is 8 hours, which is $30 + 10 = 40$ dollars.

solve.work: Every 2 hours adds 10 dollars ($5/hour). 8 hours -> 40 dollars.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: Points on the graph of a ratio relationship are written as (hours, miles): (1, 3), (2, 6) and (3, 9). How many miles go with 5 hours on this graph?
questions.solution: The points show 3 miles for every 1 hour. So 5 hours go with $5 \times 3 = 15$ miles.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: There are 100 centimeters in 1 meter. How many centimeters are in 3 meters?
questions.solution: Each meter is 100 centimeters, so 3 meters is $3 \times 100 = 300$ centimeters.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: There are 12 inches in 1 foot. A board is 5 feet long. How many inches long is the board?
questions.solution: Each foot is 12 inches, so 5 feet is $5 \times 12 = 60$ inches. (17 adds instead of multiplying, 7 subtracts, and 2.4 divides 12 by 5.)

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A bag of rice has a mass of 3000 grams. There are 1000 grams in 1 kilogram. What is the mass of the bag in kilograms?
questions.solution: Every 1000 grams make 1 kilogram, so $3000 \div 1000 = 3$ kilograms.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A box of books weighs 64 ounces. There are 16 ounces in 1 pound. How many pounds does the box weigh?
questions.solution: Every 16 ounces make 1 pound, so divide: $64 \div 16 = 4$ pounds. (48 subtracts, 1024 multiplies and 80 adds.)

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: Ben earns 8 dollars for each hour he works. The amount he earns depends on the number of hours he works. Which quantity is the independent variable?
choices: The amount of money Ben earns
The pay of 8 dollars per hour
The number of hours Ben works
questions.answer: The number of hours Ben works
questions.solution: The independent variable is the one that is chosen or changes on its own: the hours worked. The money earned depends on it, so it is the dependent variable. The 8 dollars per hour does not change.

solve.answer: The number of hours Ben works
solve.work: Earnings depend on hours, so hours is the independent variable.

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: A car travels at a steady 50 miles per hour. The equation $d = 50t$ gives the distance $d$, in miles, after $t$ hours. Which variable is the dependent variable?
questions.solution: The distance depends on how long the car travels, so $d$ is the dependent variable and $t$ is the independent variable. The speed 50 is a fixed number, not a variable.

solve.work: d = 50t: distance depends on time, so d is dependent.

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: The equation $c = 4n$ gives the cost $c$, in dollars, of $n$ notebooks. What is the cost $c$ when $n = 7$?
questions.solution: Put $n = 7$ into the equation: $c = 4 \times 7 = 28$ dollars.

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: Percent means "per 100." Which fraction is the same as 35%?
questions.solution: 35% means 35 out of every 100, which is $\frac{35}{100}$. (The fraction $\frac{100}{35}$ is upside down, and $\frac{35}{10}$ has the wrong denominator.)

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: At a school, 62 out of every 100 students ride the bus. What percent of the students ride the bus?
questions.solution: A percent is a rate per 100. 62 out of every 100 is 62 percent.

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: Which of these means the same as 8%?
questions.solution: Percent means per 100, so 8% is 8 out of every 100.

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: A store says that 30% of its 100 shirts are on sale. How many of the 100 shirts are on sale?
questions.solution: 30% means 30 out of every 100. The store has exactly 100 shirts, so 30 shirts are on sale.

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: A class has 30 students. 50% of them walk to school. How many students walk to school?
questions.solution: 50% is one half, and half of 30 is $30 \div 2 = 15$ students.

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: A box has 200 marbles. 25% of the marbles are red. How many marbles are red?
questions.solution: 25% is one fourth, so $200 \div 4 = 50$ marbles are red. (8 divides 200 by 25, 25 just repeats the percent, and 175 subtracts 25 from 200.)

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: A tank holds 400 liters of water when full. It is 10% full. How many liters of water are in the tank?
questions.solution: 10% is one tenth, so the tank holds $400 \div 10 = 40$ liters.

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: There are 50 apples in a basket. 20% of them are green. How many apples are green?
questions.solution: 20% of 50 is $\frac{20}{100} \times 50 = 10$ apples. (30 subtracts 20 from 50, 2.5 divides 50 by 20, and 70 adds.)

questions.skill: Finding the whole from a part and a percent
questions.stem: The band has 20 sixth graders. That is 50% of all the sixth graders in the school. How many sixth graders are in the school?
questions.solution: 20 is half of the sixth graders, so the whole group is twice as many: $20 \times 2 = 40$.

questions.skill: Finding the whole from a part and a percent
questions.stem: Tara has read 8 pages of her book, which is 10% of the book. How many pages are in the whole book?
questions.solution: 10% is one tenth of the book, so the whole book is 10 times as long: $8 \times 10 = 80$ pages.

questions.skill: Finding the whole from a part and a percent
questions.stem: A jar is 25% full when it has 5 cups of water in it. How many cups of water does the jar hold when it is full?
questions.solution: 25% is one fourth, so the full jar holds 4 times as much: $5 \times 4 = 20$ cups.

solve.work: 5 cups is 25% (one quarter), so full = 20 cups.

questions.skill: Finding the percent from a part and a whole
questions.stem: A bag has 20 marbles, and 5 of them are green. What percent of the marbles are green?
questions.solution: $\frac{5}{20} = \frac{25}{100}$, so 25% of the marbles are green.

questions.skill: Finding the percent from a part and a whole
questions.stem: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Amy eats 1 slice. What percent of the pizza does Amy eat?
questions.solution: 1 slice out of 4 is $\frac{1}{4} = \frac{25}{100}$, which is 25%. (75% is the part left over.)

questions.skill: Finding the percent from a part and a whole
questions.stem: A tray has 10 cookies. 3 of them are chocolate. What percent of the cookies are chocolate?
questions.solution: $\frac{3}{10} = \frac{30}{100}$, so 30% of the cookies are chocolate.

questions.skill: Finding the percent from a part and a whole
questions.stem: In a class of 25 students, 5 wear glasses. What percent of the students wear glasses?
questions.solution: $\frac{5}{25} = \frac{20}{100}$, so 20% of the students wear glasses. (80% is the part who do not.)

questions.skill: Unit conversion
questions.stem: How many inches are in 4 yards? There are 3 feet in 1 yard and 12 inches in 1 foot.
questions.solution: 4 yards is $4 \times 3 = 12$ feet. 12 feet is $12 \times 12 = 144$ inches.

questions.skill: Finding a part (percent of a price)
questions.stem: A jacket costs 40 dollars. It is on sale for 15% off. How many dollars does the sale take off the price?
questions.solution: 15% of 40 is $\frac{15}{100} \times 40 = 6$. So the sale takes off 6 dollars. (The sale price would be 40 - 6 = 34 dollars, but the question asks for the amount taken off.)

solve.work: 15% of 40 = 0.15 x 40 = 6 dollars off (sale price would be 34).

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: A plant is 5 centimeters tall and grows 2 centimeters each day. The equation $h = 5 + 2d$ gives its height $h$, in centimeters, after $d$ days. Which statement is correct?
choices: The height $h$ is the independent variable, because it is the larger number.
The number of days $d$ is the dependent variable, because it changes each day.
The height $h$ is the dependent variable, because it depends on the number of days.
Both $h$ and $d$ are independent variables, because both can be any number.
questions.answer: The height $h$ is the dependent variable, because it depends on the number of days.
questions.solution: The height is found from the number of days, so the height $h$ depends on $d$. That makes $h$ the dependent variable and $d$ the independent variable.

solve.answer: The height $h$ is the dependent variable, because it depends on the number of days.
solve.work: h = 5 + 2d: d (days) is chosen/independent; h depends on d, so h is the dependent variable. Other options give wrong roles or wrong reasons.

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table shows that 4 boxes of apples weigh 6 pounds. At this rate, how many pounds do 10 boxes of apples weigh?
questions.solution: Half of 4 boxes is 2 boxes, which weigh 3 pounds. 10 boxes is $4 + 4 + 2$ boxes, so the weight is $6 + 6 + 3 = 15$ pounds.

solve.work: 4 boxes : 6 lb = 2 : 3. 10 boxes = 5 x 2, so 5 x 3 = 15 lb.

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table lists three rows of (liters of paint, square meters covered): the first is 2 and 18, the second is 5 and a missing number, and the third is 10 and 90. What is the missing number?
questions.solution: Each liter covers $18 \div 2 = 9$ square meters, so 5 liters cover $5 \times 9 = 45$ square meters. (The number 9 is the amount for 1 liter, and 21 comes from adding 3 to 18.) This also fits the third row, since 10 liters cover 90.

solve.work: 18/2 = 9 sq m per liter; 90/10 = 9 too. 5 liters -> 45.

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table for filling a pool has two rows. One row is 3 minutes and 24 gallons. The other row has a missing number of minutes and 72 gallons. How many minutes are in the missing row?
questions.solution: 72 gallons is $72 \div 24 = 3$ times as much as 24 gallons, so it takes 3 times as long: $3 \times 3 = 9$ minutes.

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: Dee makes green paint by mixing 3 parts blue with 4 parts yellow. She uses 12 cups of yellow. How many cups of blue does she use?
questions.solution: 12 cups of yellow is $12 \div 4 = 3$ times the 4 parts, so she needs 3 times the 3 parts of blue: $3 \times 3 = 9$ cups.

solve.work: Blue:yellow = 3:4. 12 yellow = 4 x 3, so blue = 3 x 3 = 9.

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: Which ratio is NOT equivalent to 6 to 8?
questions.solution: 6 to 8 simplifies to 3 to 4. Both 9 to 12 and 12 to 16 also simplify to 3 to 4, but 7 to 9 does not (it is already in simplest form and is a different ratio).

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: The ratio of red marbles to blue marbles in a bag is 1 to 3. There are 24 marbles in all. How many marbles are red?
questions.solution: 1 part red and 3 parts blue make 4 equal parts in all. Each part is $24 \div 4 = 6$ marbles, so 6 marbles are red.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: A double number line pairs hours worked (top) with dollars earned (bottom). The top marks are 0, 2, 4 and 6, and the bottom marks are 0, 18, 36 and 54. How many hours match 90 dollars?
questions.solution: Every 2 hours earn 18 dollars, so 1 hour earns 9 dollars. Then 90 dollars takes $90 \div 9 = 10$ hours.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: The graph of a ratio relationship between feet of ribbon and its cost in dollars contains the points (3, 12) and (5, 20), written as (feet, dollars). What is the cost, in dollars, of 8 feet of ribbon?
questions.solution: From the point (3, 12), each foot costs $12 \div 3 = 4$ dollars (the point (5, 20) agrees). So 8 feet cost $8 \times 4 = 32$ dollars.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: The graph of a ratio relationship contains the points (2, 5) and (4, 10), written as (cups of flour, cups of sugar). Which point is also on the graph?
questions.solution: The sugar is always $\frac{5}{2}$ times the flour. For 6 cups of flour, $6 \times \frac{5}{2} = 15$. So (6, 15) is on the graph. (6, 13) comes from adding 3 to 10, and (6, 12) uses a ratio of 2.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A pitcher holds 2.5 liters of juice. There are 1000 milliliters in 1 liter. How many milliliters of juice does the pitcher hold?
questions.solution: Each liter is 1000 milliliters, so 2.5 liters is $2.5 \times 1000 = 2500$ milliliters.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: There are 2 pints in 1 quart and 4 quarts in 1 gallon. How many pints are in 3 gallons?
questions.solution: 3 gallons is $3 \times 4 = 12$ quarts, and 12 quarts is $12 \times 2 = 24$ pints. (12 stops at quarts, 6 skips the quarts, and 9 adds.)

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A video is 150 minutes long. There are 60 minutes in 1 hour. How many hours long is the video? Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: $150 \div 60 = 2.5$ hours. Check: 2 hours is 120 minutes and the other 30 minutes is half an hour.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A hose delivers 3 liters of water each minute. There are 60 minutes in 1 hour. How many liters of water does the hose deliver in 1 hour?
questions.solution: In 1 hour there are 60 minutes, and the hose delivers 3 liters in each one: $3 \times 60 = 180$ liters. (63 adds, 20 divides 60 by 3, and 0.05 divides 3 by 60.)

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: A gym charges a sign-up fee of 20 dollars plus 5 dollars for each visit. The total cost $c$, in dollars, depends on the number of visits $v$. Which equation shows this relationship?
questions.solution: Each visit costs 5 dollars, so $v$ visits cost $5v$. The sign-up fee of 20 dollars is paid once, so the total is $c = 5v + 20$.

solve.work: Cost = 5 per visit times v plus 20 fee: c = 5v + 20.

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: The equation $c = 12 + 3n$ gives the cost $c$, in dollars, of renting skates for $n$ hours: a fee of 12 dollars plus 3 dollars for each hour. What is the cost, in dollars, for 5 hours?
questions.solution: Put $n = 5$ into the equation: $c = 12 + 3 \times 5 = 12 + 15 = 27$ dollars.

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: A bus travels the same number of miles each hour. When the number of hours $h$ is 1, 2, 3 and 4, the total miles $m$ is 45, 90, 135 and 180. Which equation matches these values, with $m$ depending on $h$?
questions.solution: Each hour adds 45 miles, and $m$ is 45 times $h$ every time: $45 \times 3 = 135$. The equation $m = 45h$ fits. The others fail, for example $m = 45 + h$ gives 47 when $h = 2$.

solve.work: m/h = 45 each time, so m = 45h. m = 45 + h gives 46 at h=1; h = 45m reversed; m = h + 44 gives 46 at h=2.

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: Which fraction in simplest form is the same as 40%?
questions.solution: 40% is $\frac{40}{100}$. Divide the top and bottom by 20 to get $\frac{2}{5}$.

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: In a survey, 9 out of every 25 people chose pears. At the same rate, how many out of every 100 people would choose pears?
questions.solution: 100 is 4 times 25, so multiply 9 by 4: $9 \times 4 = 36$ out of every 100 (which is 36%).

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: The sales tax in a town is 6%. As a decimal, what number is the same as 6%? Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: 6% means 6 per 100, which is $\frac{6}{100} = 0.06$.

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: The bill at a restaurant is 60 dollars. Zoe leaves a 15% tip. How many dollars is the tip?
questions.solution: 10% of 60 is 6 and 5% is 3, so 15% is $6 + 3 = 9$ dollars. (4 divides 60 by 15, 45 subtracts, and 900 multiplies without dividing by 100.)

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: A school has 480 students. 35% of them take the bus. How many students take the bus?
questions.solution: 35% of 480 is $\frac{35}{100} \times 480 = 0.35 \times 480 = 168$ students.

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: A water bottle holds 64 ounces. It is 75% full. How many ounces of water are in the bottle?
questions.solution: 75% is three fourths, and $64 \div 4 = 16$, so $3 \times 16 = 48$ ounces. (16 is only one fourth.)

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: In a class of 28 students, 25% are left-handed. How many students are left-handed?
questions.solution: 25% is one fourth, so $28 \div 4 = 7$ students are left-handed. (21 is the number who are not, 3 subtracts and 53 adds.)

questions.skill: Finding a part: percent of a quantity
questions.stem: A test has 45 questions. Kim answered 80% of them correctly. How many questions did she answer correctly?
questions.solution: 80% of 45 is $0.8 \times 45 = 36$ questions.

questions.skill: Finding the whole from a part and a percent
questions.stem: A store sold 18 bikes this week. That was 30% of all the bikes in the store. How many bikes were in the store?
questions.solution: 30% of the bikes is 18, so 10% is $18 \div 3 = 6$ bikes. The whole is 100%, which is $6 \times 10 = 60$ bikes.

questions.skill: Finding the whole from a part and a percent
questions.stem: A sweater is on sale for 12 dollars off. This is 20% of the original price. What was the original price, in dollars?
questions.solution: 20% is one fifth of the price, so the whole price is 5 times 12: $12 \times 5 = 60$ dollars.

questions.skill: Finding the whole from a part and a percent
questions.stem: The school band has 45 students. That is 15% of all the students at the school. How many students are at the school?
questions.solution: 15% of the students is 45, so 5% is $45 \div 3 = 15$. The whole school is 100%, which is $15 \times 20 = 300$ students. (3 forgets to multiply by 100.)

questions.skill: Finding the percent from a part and a whole
questions.stem: A basketball player made 18 of her 24 free throws. What percent of her free throws did she make?
questions.solution: $\frac{18}{24} = \frac{3}{4} = \frac{75}{100}$, so she made 75%. (25% is the part she missed.)

questions.skill: Finding the percent from a part and a whole
questions.stem: A tank held 40 liters of water. After a day, 14 liters had been used. What percent of the water had been used?
questions.solution: $\frac{14}{40} = \frac{35}{100}$, so 35% of the water had been used. (65% is the part left.)

questions.skill: Finding the percent from a part and a whole
questions.stem: A town has 250 people, and 90 of them are children. What percent of the people in the town are children?
questions.solution: Since $250 \times 0.4 = 100$, multiply 90 by 0.4 too: $90 \times 0.4 = 36$. So $\frac{90}{250} = \frac{36}{100}$, and 36% of the people are children.

questions.skill: Finding the whole from a part and a percent
questions.stem: Jordan has read 36 pages, which is 40% of a book. How many pages are in the whole book?
questions.solution: 40% of the book is 36 pages, so 10% is $36 \div 4 = 9$ pages. The whole book is 100%, which is $9 \times 10 = 90$ pages.

solve.work: 36 = 40% of total. 10% = 9, so 100% = 90 pages. Check 0.4 x 90 = 36.

questions.skill: Rate and unit conversion
questions.stem: A cyclist rides at a steady speed of 12 miles per hour. How many miles does the cyclist ride in 45 minutes?
questions.solution: 45 minutes is $\frac{45}{60} = \frac{3}{4}$ of an hour. Then $\frac{3}{4} \times 12 = 9$ miles.

questions.skill: Ratio problem with a total
questions.stem: Grape juice and apple juice are mixed in the ratio 3 to 5. A pitcher holds 40 cups of the mix. How many cups of the mix are grape juice?
questions.solution: Each batch of the mix has $3 + 5 = 8$ parts, and 3 of the 8 parts are grape. $40 \div 8 = 5$ cups per part, so grape juice is $3 \times 5 = 15$ cups.

solve.work: Ratio 3:5, 8 parts total. 40 / 8 = 5 cups per part. Grape = 3 x 5 = 15 cups.

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table shows that a car uses 6 gallons of gas to drive 156 miles. Using the same ratio, how many miles can the car drive on 15 gallons of gas?
questions.solution: The car drives $156 \div 6 = 26$ miles on each gallon, so 15 gallons take it $15 \times 26 = 390$ miles. (182 adds 26 to 156, and 2340 multiplies 156 by 15 without dividing.)

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table has the rows 5 to 12 and 15 to 36. Which row could also be in this table?
questions.solution: The second number is always $\frac{12}{5} = 2.4$ times the first. For 10 the partner is $10 \times 2.4 = 24$. The other rows add the same amount to both numbers, which does not keep the ratio.

solve.work: 5:12, 15:36 (x3). 10:24 (x2) fits. 25:32, 20:27, 10:17 do not (25 would need 60, 20 would need 48, 10 would need 24).

questions.skill: Ratio table: finding a missing value
questions.stem: A ratio table shows that 6 muffins use 4 cups of flour. How many cups of flour are used to make 21 muffins?
questions.solution: 3 muffins use 2 cups, and 21 muffins is 7 groups of 3 muffins, so $7 \times 2 = 14$ cups. (19 adds 15 to both numbers, 31.5 inverts the ratio, and 126 multiplies 6 by 21.)

solve.work: 6 muffins : 4 cups = 3 : 2. 21 = 7 x 3, so 7 x 2 = 14 cups.

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: The ratio of dogs to cats at a shelter is 5 to 3. There are 6 more dogs than cats. How many dogs are at the shelter?
questions.solution: Dogs are 5 parts and cats are 3 parts, so the difference is $5 - 3 = 2$ parts. 2 parts is 6 animals, so 1 part is 3. Dogs are $5 \times 3 = 15$ (and cats are 9).

solve.work: Dogs - cats = 5 - 3 = 2 parts = 6, so 1 part = 3. Dogs = 5 x 3 = 15 (cats 9, difference 6).

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: Mix A uses 3 cups of juice for every 5 cups of water. Mix B uses 2 cups of juice for every 3 cups of water. Which statement is true?
choices: Mix B tastes more strongly of juice than Mix A
Mix A tastes more strongly of juice than Mix B
The two mixes taste equally of juice
Mix A is stronger because 3 is greater than 2
questions.answer: Mix B tastes more strongly of juice than Mix A
questions.solution: Compare the juice for the same 15 cups of water. Mix A: 3 to 5 is 9 to 15. Mix B: 2 to 3 is 10 to 15. Mix B has more juice for the same water, so it is stronger.

solve.answer: Mix B tastes more strongly of juice than Mix A
solve.work: A: juice per water 3/5 = 0.6 (juice fraction 3/8 = 0.375). B: 2/3 = 0.667 (2/5 = 0.4). B has more juice per cup of water, so B is stronger.

questions.skill: Equivalent ratios in a context
questions.stem: Red, blue and white paint are mixed in the ratio 2 to 3 to 5. A mix uses 8 cups of red paint. How many cups of paint are in the mix altogether?
questions.solution: 2 parts of red is 8 cups, so 1 part is 4 cups. The mix has $2 + 3 + 5 = 10$ parts, so it has $10 \times 4 = 40$ cups.

solve.work: Red 2 parts = 8, so 1 part = 4. Total parts 2+3+5 = 10, so 40 cups.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: On a double number line, the top line shows minutes and the bottom line shows pages read. The top marks 0, 10, 20 and 30 are paired with the bottom marks 0, 6, 12 and 18. How many minutes does it take to read 45 pages at this rate?
questions.solution: Reading 6 pages takes 10 minutes, so 1 page takes $\frac{10}{6} = \frac{5}{3}$ minutes. Then 45 pages take $45 \times \frac{5}{3} = 75$ minutes.

solve.work: 10 min : 6 pages = 5 : 3. 45 pages = 15 x 3, so 15 x 5 = 75 minutes.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: The graph of the relationship between gallons of gas and miles driven is a straight line through (0, 0) and (5, 120), where each point is (gallons, miles). How many gallons are needed to drive 288 miles?
questions.solution: The line shows $120 \div 5 = 24$ miles for each gallon. So 288 miles need $288 \div 24 = 12$ gallons.

questions.skill: Double number line or graph of a ratio
questions.stem: Each answer gives two points. Which pair of points CANNOT both be on the graph of one ratio relationship that passes through (0, 0)?
questions.solution: On such a graph, the second number divided by the first is always the same. (2, 3) and (4, 6) give 1.5 and 1.5; (1, 5) and (3, 15) give 5 and 5; (2, 6) and (5, 15) give 3 and 3. But (2, 4) gives 2 and (3, 9) gives 3, so they do not match.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A leaky faucet loses 25 milliliters of water every minute. There are 1000 milliliters in 1 liter and 60 minutes in 1 hour. How many liters of water does it lose in 2 hours?
questions.solution: 2 hours is $2 \times 60 = 120$ minutes, so the faucet loses $25 \times 120 = 3000$ milliliters. That is $3000 \div 1000 = 3$ liters.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: There are 100 centimeters in 1 meter and 1000 meters in 1 kilometer. Which length is the longest?
questions.solution: Change each to meters: 5000 centimeters is 50 meters; 40 meters is 40 meters; 0.06 kilometers is 60 meters; 0.045 kilometers is 45 meters. The longest is 60 meters, which is 0.06 kilometers.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A 3-pound bag of rice is split into servings of 6 ounces each. There are 16 ounces in 1 pound. How many servings are in the bag?
questions.solution: 3 pounds is $3 \times 16 = 48$ ounces. Each serving is 6 ounces, so there are $48 \div 6 = 8$ servings.

questions.skill: Converting units with ratio reasoning
questions.stem: A runner runs at a steady 6 meters per second. There are 60 seconds in 1 minute and 1000 meters in 1 kilometer. How many kilometers does the runner run in 10 minutes?
questions.solution: 10 minutes is $10 \times 60 = 600$ seconds, so the runner covers $6 \times 600 = 3600$ meters. That is $3600 \div 1000 = 3.6$ kilometers.

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: The equation $T = 60 + 12n$ gives the total savings $T$, in dollars, after $n$ weeks. After how many weeks will the total savings be 144 dollars?
questions.solution: Set $T = 144$: $60 + 12n = 144$, so $12n = 84$ and $n = 7$ weeks. (12 divides 144 by 12 without taking away the starting 60, and 84 stops one step early.)

solve.issues: Minor: solving 60 + 12n = 144 is a two-step equation (more grade 7), though the options can be checked by substitution.

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: In which situation is the number of hours the dependent variable?
choices: The money a tutor earns depends on the hours tutored
The miles a bus drives depend on the hours it drives
The hours needed to mow a lawn depend on the number of mowers
The pages a student reads depend on the hours of reading
questions.answer: The hours needed to mow a lawn depend on the number of mowers
questions.solution: In the first situation the number of hours depends on how many people mow, so hours is the dependent variable. In each of the others the hours are chosen first and the other quantity depends on them.

solve.answer: The hours needed to mow a lawn depend on the number of mowers
solve.work: Mowing: hours depend on mowers, so hours is dependent. In the other three, hours is the independent variable.

questions.skill: Independent and dependent variables
questions.stem: A table shows values of $x$ and $y$. When $x$ is 2, $y$ is 11. When $x$ is 4, $y$ is 19. When $x$ is 6, $y$ is 27. Each time $x$ goes up by 2, $y$ goes up by the same amount. What is $y$ when $x$ is 10?
questions.solution: $y$ goes up by 8 each time $x$ goes up by 2 ($11, 19, 27$). From $x = 6$ to $x = 10$ is two more steps: $27 + 8 + 8 = 43$.

solve.issues: Minor: a non-proportional linear pattern, only loosely tied to ratio reasoning.

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
questions.stem: Which of these is NOT equal to 15%?
questions.solution: 15% means $\frac{15}{100} = 0.15$, and $\frac{15}{100} = \frac{3}{20}$. The number 1.5 is 150%, so it is not equal to 15%.

questions.skill: Percent as a rate per 100
