solve.answer: A random sample of 80 students, which is 1 out of every 10 students
solve.work: All random; the largest (80) gives the most reliable picture.

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: Kofi wants to answer the question "How many letters are in the first names of the students in my grade?" What should he record for each student?
choices: The student's favorite letter of the alphabet to write down
The number of students in the grade who have first names
The student's age in years on the day of the survey
The number of letters in each student's own first name
questions.answer: The number of letters in each student's own first name
questions.solution: To answer the question, he needs one number for each student: how many letters are in that student's first name. The other things are not what the question asks about.

solve.answer: The number of letters in each student's own first name
solve.work: Answering the question needs the number of letters in each student's first name.

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: Lena wants to answer "How far do the students in my class live from school?" What should she record for each student?
choices: The distance from the student's home to school, in miles
The student's favorite way to travel to school, such as bus or walking
The total number of students in the class, as a number such as 24 students
The color of the student's backpack that is carried to school each day
questions.answer: The distance from the student's home to school, in miles
questions.solution: The question is about distance, so Lena records how far each student's home is from school. The other choices record things the question does not ask about.

solve.answer: The distance from the student's home to school, in miles
solve.work: The distance from home to school for each student answers 'how far'.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased survey question
questions.stem: Mr. Cole wants to know where students like to read. Which survey question is worded in a way that pushes people toward one answer?
choices: Where do you like to read best: the library, a classroom, or home?
Everyone loves the fantastic new library, so isn't it the best place to read?
How many times a week do you read at the library?
What is your favorite place to read?
questions.answer: Everyone loves the fantastic new library, so isn't it the best place to read?
questions.solution: The question that says "Everyone loves the fantastic new library" tells people what answer to give, so it is biased. The other questions are neutral.

solve.answer: Everyone loves the fantastic new library, so isn't it the best place to read?
solve.work: The question that states 'Everyone loves the fantastic new library' leads respondents to agree; it is the biased one.

questions.skill: Organizing survey results in a frequency table
questions.stem: A survey of 25 students asked how many brothers and sisters each has. The results were: 0 siblings, 4 students; 1 sibling, 9 students; 2 siblings, 8 students; 3 siblings, 4 students. How many students have at least 2 siblings?
questions.solution: "At least 2" means 2 or more. Add the students with 2 siblings and with 3 siblings: $8 + 4 = 12$ students.

solve.work: At least 2 siblings: 2 siblings (8) + 3 siblings (4) = 12. Totals check: 4 + 9 + 8 + 4 = 25.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative sample
questions.stem: A school has 600 students. The principal wants to know the favorite lunch of all students. Which way of choosing 40 students to ask is most likely to give a representative sample?
choices: Ask the first 40 students in the pizza line
Ask the 40 students on the soccer team
Ask 40 students who volunteer in the cafeteria
Choose 40 names at random from a list of all students
questions.answer: Choose 40 names at random from a list of all students
questions.solution: A random choice from the list of everyone gives every student the same chance of being asked. The other groups all favor certain kinds of students.

solve.answer: Choose 40 names at random from a list of all students
solve.work: A random selection from the full list gives every student an equal chance; the other methods are biased groups.

questions.skill: Telling a statistical question from other questions
questions.stem: A neighborhood group is studying traffic near the school. Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: How many lanes does the road in front of the school have?
What is the speed limit on the road in front of the school?
How many cars pass the school each hour during the morning?
How many cars are parked outside the school right now?
questions.answer: How many cars pass the school each hour during the morning?
questions.solution: The number of cars passing changes from hour to hour, so answering the question takes data from many hours. The number of lanes and the speed limit are single facts, and the number of cars parked right now is one count at one moment.

solve.answer: How many cars pass the school each hour during the morning?
solve.work: Lanes, speed limit and cars parked right now each have one answer. Cars passing each hour during the morning varies hour to hour/day to day: statistical.

questions.skill: Telling a statistical question from other questions
questions.stem: A coach writes five questions. 1. How many goals did the team score in each game this season? 2. How many goals did Dev score in last Friday's game? 3. How long does it take each player to run one lap of the track? 4. How many players are on the team's roster today? 5. How far does each player live from school, in miles? How many of the five questions are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Questions 1, 3 and 5 expect different answers from game to game or player to player, so they are statistical. Question 2 asks about one player in one game and question 4 has one answer. That makes 3 statistical questions.

solve.work: 1: goals in each game vary across games -> yes. 2: one player, one game -> no. 3: lap time of each player varies -> yes. 4: roster today is one number -> no. 5: distance for each player varies -> yes. Count = 3.

questions.skill: Population and sample
questions.stem: A town has $8{,}000$ residents. A survey about the new library hours is given to 200 of them. How many residents are in the population but not in the sample?
questions.solution: The population is all $8{,}000$ residents and the sample is 200 of them. Residents not in the sample number $8{,}000 - 200 = 7{,}800$.

questions.skill: Population and sample
questions.stem: A researcher wants to learn about the heights of all the sixth graders in North Carolina. She measures 150 sixth graders from five schools. Which statement is correct?
choices: The 150 sixth graders are the population, and all sixth graders in North Carolina are the sample.
The five schools are the population, and the 150 sixth graders are the sample.
All sixth graders in North Carolina are the population, and the 150 she measures are a sample.
The heights are the population, and the 150 sixth graders are the sample.
questions.answer: All sixth graders in North Carolina are the population, and the 150 she measures are a sample.
questions.solution: The population is the whole group she wants to learn about, which is all sixth graders in North Carolina. The 150 students she measures are a part of that group, so they are a sample.

solve.answer: All sixth graders in North Carolina are the population, and the 150 she measures are a sample.
solve.work: Population: all NC sixth graders; sample: the 150 measured. C.

questions.skill: Population and sample
questions.stem: A factory makes $2{,}400$ light bulbs in a day. An inspector tests 1 out of every 20 bulbs. How many bulbs are in the inspector's sample?
questions.solution: Testing 1 out of every 20 bulbs means one twentieth of the bulbs. $2{,}400 \div 20 = 120$ bulbs.

solve.work: 1 of every 20 bulbs: 2400 / 20 = 120 bulbs in the sample.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased survey question
questions.stem: A survey asks, "How much do you enjoy our wonderful school library?" Which rewording takes the bias out?
choices: How would you rate our school library: poor, fair, good or excellent?
How much do you enjoy our school library, which has the best books in town?
How much do you love our school library?
How wonderful is our school library to you?
questions.answer: How would you rate our school library: poor, fair, good or excellent?
questions.solution: The word "wonderful" pushes people toward a positive answer. The rewording that offers a range of ratings, from poor to excellent, does not hint at an answer. The others keep or add words that push toward a high opinion.

solve.answer: How would you rate our school library: poor, fair, good or excellent?
solve.work: A "love" and D "wonderful" still lead; C adds praise. B gives a balanced rating scale with no loaded word.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased survey question
questions.stem: A club asks five survey questions about hiking. 1. Do you prefer hiking, biking or swimming? 2. Do you agree that hiking is boring and nobody likes it? 3. How many times did you go hiking last month? 4. Isn't swimming way better than hiking? 5. Hiking is great exercise, isn't it? How many of the five questions are biased?
questions.solution: Questions 2, 4 and 5 are worded to push people toward one answer. Questions 1 and 3 are fair. That makes 3 biased questions.

solve.work: 1 neutral. 2 leading ("boring and nobody likes it"). 3 neutral count. 4 leading ("Isn't swimming way better"). 5 leading ("great exercise, isn't it"). Biased = 3.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased way of choosing a sample
questions.stem: A school wants to know what lunch time students prefer. Which plan is MOST likely to give a biased sample?
choices: Ask every 10th student on an alphabetical list of all students
Draw 50 names from a box holding every student's name
Ask only the students who are first in the lunch line
Ask 10 students chosen at random from each grade
questions.answer: Ask only the students who are first in the lunch line
questions.solution: Students who are first in the lunch line are probably the ones who prefer an early lunch, so the sample leaves out other students' opinions. The other plans give every student a fair chance of being asked.

solve.answer: Ask only the students who are first in the lunch line
solve.work: B, C, D are systematic/random. First students in the lunch line are a convenience group (e.g. hungriest or earliest), likely biased: A.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased way of choosing a sample
questions.stem: A school has 400 students, and 90 of them ride a bus. Pablo surveys only the students waiting at the bus stop. What fraction of the school's students could possibly be in his sample? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Only the 90 bus riders can be in the sample. The fraction is $\frac{90}{400} = \frac{9}{40}$, so most students have no chance of being asked.

solve.work: Only bus riders wait at the bus stop: 90 of 400. 90/400 = 9/40.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative or random sample
questions.stem: A school has 300 sixth graders, 200 seventh graders and 100 eighth graders. The principal wants a sample of 60 students whose grades match the school's. How many of the 60 should be sixth graders?
questions.solution: The school has $300 + 200 + 100 = 600$ students, and sixth graders are $\frac{300}{600} = \frac{1}{2}$ of them. Half of the 60 students in the sample should be sixth graders: $\frac{1}{2} \times 60 = 30$.

questions.skill: Sample size and the share of the population asked
questions.stem: A club has 80 members. A sample must include at least 10% of the members. What is the smallest number of members that can be in the sample?
questions.solution: 10% of 80 is $0.1 \times 80 = 8$, so the sample needs at least 8 members.

solve.work: 10% of 80 = 8; the sample must be at least 8, so the smallest is 8.

questions.skill: Sample size and the share of the population asked
questions.stem: A school has 600 students. Each day for 3 days, 20 new students are asked a question, and no student is asked twice. What percent of the school has been asked?
questions.solution: In 3 days, $3 \times 20 = 60$ students are asked. $\frac{60}{600} = 10\%$ of the school.

questions.skill: Organizing data in a frequency table
questions.stem: A soccer team's goals in its 15 games were 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2, 1, 0, 4, 2, 1, 3, 2, 0, 1. Ana puts them in a frequency table. In how many games did the team score more than 1 goal?
questions.solution: Make the frequency table: 0 goals, 3 games; 1 goal, 4 games; 2 goals, 5 games; 3 goals, 2 games; 4 goals, 1 game. Games with more than 1 goal: $5 + 2 + 1 = 8$.

questions.skill: Organizing data in a frequency table
questions.stem: A frequency table shows the number of pets owned by 30 students: 0 pets, 6 students; 1 pet, 11 students; 2 pets, a number not shown; 3 pets, 4 students. How many students own exactly 2 pets?
questions.solution: The rows must add to 30. Students in the other rows: $6 + 11 + 4 = 21$. So $30 - 21 = 9$ students own 2 pets.

questions.skill: Organizing data in a frequency table
questions.stem: A frequency table groups the minutes 23 students spent on a project: 0 to 9 minutes, 4 students; 10 to 19 minutes, 9 students; 20 to 29 minutes, 7 students; 30 to 39 minutes, 3 students. How many students spent fewer than 20 minutes?
questions.solution: Students who spent fewer than 20 minutes are in the first two groups: $4 + 9 = 13$ students.

questions.skill: Organizing survey results as fractions and percents
questions.stem: Eli surveyed 40 students about their favorite subject. Math got 14 votes, science got 10 votes, art got 8 votes and the rest chose reading. What fraction of the students chose reading? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Reading got $40 - 14 - 10 - 8 = 8$ votes. The fraction is $\frac{8}{40} = \frac{1}{5}$.

questions.skill: Organizing survey results as fractions and percents
questions.stem: In a survey of 80 students, 35% chose pizza as their favorite lunch. How many students chose pizza?
questions.solution: 35% of 80 is $0.35 \times 80 = 28$ students.

questions.skill: Organizing survey results as fractions and percents
questions.stem: Twenty-five students were asked which fruit they like best. Ten said apple, 8 said orange and 7 said banana. What percent of the students said banana?

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: Zoe records the hours of sleep of 16 students: 7, 8, 9, 8, 7, 8, 10, 8, 9, 7, 8, 9, 8, 10, 7, 8. She makes a frequency table with one row for each different value. How many rows does the table have?
questions.solution: The different values are 7, 8, 9 and 10, so the table has 4 rows.

questions.skill: Telling a statistical question from other questions
questions.stem: Mr. Ito asks, "How tall are the students in my class?" Which statement best explains why this is a statistical question?
choices: It asks about a number, and every question that asks about a number is a statistical question
It can be answered by measuring just one student, such as the tallest student in the class
It has a single answer that never changes, no matter which students are measured
The students' heights will vary, so it takes data from many different students to answer it
questions.answer: The students' heights will vary, so it takes data from many different students to answer it
questions.solution: A statistical question has answers that vary, so it can only be answered by collecting data from many members of a group. Students have different heights. Asking about a number is not enough, because "How many days are in a week?" asks about a number but has one answer.

solve.answer: The students' heights will vary, so it takes data from many different students to answer it
solve.work: A statistical question anticipates variability; heights vary, so data from many students are needed.

questions.skill: Choosing a statistical question that fits a situation
questions.stem: A store manager recorded how many customers came in during each hour of one day. Which statistical question can be answered with these data?
choices: How much does the store pay each of its workers for one hour of work?
How many customers come into the store in each hour that it is open?
What is the price of a loaf of bread that the store sells on this day?
How many loaves of bread are on the shelf at the start of the day?
questions.answer: How many customers come into the store in each hour that it is open?
questions.solution: The data are a number of customers for each hour, and the number changes from hour to hour, so they answer the question about customers in an hour. Pay, prices and bread on the shelf would need other data.

solve.answer: How many customers come into the store in each hour that it is open?
solve.work: Hourly customer counts answer how many customers come in each hour; others need prices/pay/stock.

questions.skill: Choosing a statistical question that fits a situation
questions.stem: Eli wants to ask a statistical question about the sixth graders at his school. Which question is the best choice?
choices: How many minutes does it take me to get to school from my home on a normal morning?
What time does school start for the sixth graders at my school each morning?
How many minutes are in a regular school day at my school, from start to end?
How many minutes does it take sixth graders at my school to get to school?
questions.answer: How many minutes does it take sixth graders at my school to get to school?
questions.solution: The travel times of the sixth graders will vary, so the question needs data from many of them, and it is about the group Eli chose. The others ask about Eli alone or have a single answer.

solve.answer: How many minutes does it take sixth graders at my school to get to school?
solve.work: Travel time of sixth graders varies across students; others are about Eli alone or fixed facts.

questions.skill: Choosing a statistical question that fits a situation
questions.stem: Six students did as many push-ups as they could in one minute. The data are 9, 12, 8, 15, 11, 10. Which statistical question could these data help answer?
choices: How many push-ups can the students in this group do in one minute of exercise?
How many minutes long is a gym class for the students in this group?
How many students joined the gym club at the start of this school year?
How many push-ups did the coach do while the students were counting?
questions.answer: How many push-ups can the students in this group do in one minute of exercise?
questions.solution: The data are numbers of push-ups from different students, so they help answer a question about how many push-ups students can do in a minute. The class length, the gym club and the coach are not in the data.

solve.answer: How many push-ups can the students in this group do in one minute of exercise?
solve.work: Push-up counts per student answer how many push-ups the students can do in a minute.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased survey question
questions.stem: A town wants to know whether residents support a new playground. Which survey question is biased?
choices: Do you support building a new playground in town, or would you rather it not be built?
How do you feel about a new playground in town: are you for it, against it or still unsure?
Since playgrounds keep children safe and happy, do you support building a new one?
Should the town build a new playground, build something else or build nothing at all?
questions.answer: Since playgrounds keep children safe and happy, do you support building a new one?
questions.solution: The question that begins "Since playgrounds keep children safe and happy" gives a reason to say yes before asking, which pushes people toward supporting the playground. The other three questions let people choose without a hint about which answer is better.

solve.answer: Since playgrounds keep children safe and happy, do you support building a new one?
solve.work: Giving a one-sided reason (keep children safe and happy) leads respondents; others are balanced.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased way of choosing a sample
questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in and vote for the best pizza topping in town. Why is the result likely to be biased?
choices: The station asked far too many people, so there are too many votes to give a fair picture of the town
Pizza toppings are only a matter of taste, so a survey cannot give a fair picture of what the town likes
The station asked listeners instead of every single person in town, so no vote of this kind can be fair
Only listeners who care enough to call will answer, so the sample is not a fair picture of everyone in town
questions.answer: Only listeners who care enough to call will answer, so the sample is not a fair picture of everyone in town
questions.solution: When people choose for themselves whether to answer, only those with strong opinions or time to call will answer. They may not match everyone in town.

solve.answer: Only listeners who care enough to call will answer, so the sample is not a fair picture of everyone in town
solve.work: Voluntary call-in response: only motivated listeners respond, not representative.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative or random sample
questions.stem: A park wants to know how visitors rate its new trail. Which plan is most likely to give a representative sample of visitors?
choices: Ask the visitors who stop at the snack stand near the trail on a sunny Saturday
Ask every 5th visitor who enters the park, on several different days of the week
Ask only the visitors who are on the trail on a rainy Monday morning in the spring
Ask the first 20 visitors who arrive at the park gate on a Saturday morning
questions.answer: Ask every 5th visitor who enters the park, on several different days of the week
questions.solution: Asking every 5th visitor on different days spreads the sample across all kinds of visitors and days. The other plans ask only certain visitors, such as snack-stand customers or visitors on one day.

solve.answer: Ask every 5th visitor who enters the park, on several different days of the week
solve.work: Systematic every-5th visitor across several days covers varied visitors; others are restricted by weather/time/location.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative or random sample
questions.stem: A middle school has sixth, seventh and eighth graders, with about the same number in each grade. To learn about the whole school, which sample is best?
choices: 30 students chosen at random from the sixth-grade list alone
10 students chosen at random from every one of the grade lists
The 30 students who finish a test first, from any of the grades
The 30 students in the school choir, who come from all of the grades
questions.answer: 10 students chosen at random from every one of the grade lists
questions.solution: A good sample includes all three grades and chooses students at random. The other samples come from only one grade or from a special group, so they would not match the whole school.

solve.answer: 10 students chosen at random from every one of the grade lists
solve.work: 10 random from each grade covers all grades equally and randomly; others are one grade or self-selected groups.

questions.skill: Sample size and the share of the population asked
questions.stem: Dara and Eli each choose a random sample of students at their school to estimate how many students like soccer. Dara asks 8 students and Eli asks 80 students. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: Dara's results are likely to be better because 8 students are easier to count and ask
Eli's results, from the larger random sample, are likely to give a better picture of the whole school
The two results must be exactly the same, because both samples were chosen at random
Neither sample can tell anything about the school, because both are smaller than the whole school
questions.answer: Eli's results, from the larger random sample, are likely to give a better picture of the whole school
questions.solution: Both samples are random, so both can tell something about the school. The larger random sample usually matches the population more closely, so Eli's results are likely to be better.

solve.answer: Eli's results, from the larger random sample, are likely to give a better picture of the whole school
solve.work: Larger random sample tends to estimate the population better; results need not match exactly.

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: The student council wants to answer "How many days a week do students buy school lunch?" Which way of recording the data is best?
choices: Write only yes or no for whether each student buys lunch
Write the name of the lunch that is each student's favorite
Write the price of the lunch that each student pays on a school day
Write the number of days, from 0 to 5, that each student buys school lunch
questions.answer: Write the number of days, from 0 to 5, that each student buys school lunch
questions.solution: The question asks for a number of days, so each student's number from 0 to 5 gives the data needed. Yes or no, a favorite lunch and a price do not tell how many days.

solve.answer: Write the number of days, from 0 to 5, that each student buys school lunch
solve.work: Recording 0-5 days per student directly answers how many days a week.

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: A class records the favorite pizza topping of each student. Which question can they answer with these data?
choices: How many slices of pizza do the students in our class eat in a week?
How much does a pizza cost at the shop near our school?
Which toppings do the students in our class like best on a pizza?
How long does it take to bake a pizza in a hot oven?
questions.answer: Which toppings do the students in our class like best on a pizza?
questions.solution: The data show which topping each student likes best, so they answer a question about favorite toppings. The number of pizzas eaten, the cost and the baking time are not in the data.

solve.answer: Which toppings do the students in our class like best on a pizza?
solve.work: Favorite topping data answers which toppings students like best.

questions.skill: A large sample can still be biased
questions.stem: Ruth wants to know which sport is the favorite of the people in her town. Plan A is to ask 500 people leaving a basketball game. Plan B is to ask 50 people chosen at random from a list of all the town's residents. Which statement is true?
choices: Plan B is better, because a random sample is more likely to represent the whole town
Plan A is better, because a larger sample is always more representative
Plan A is better, because basketball fans know the most about sports
The plans are equally good, because both ask people
questions.answer: Plan B is better, because a random sample is more likely to represent the whole town
questions.solution: People leaving a basketball game are probably more likely than other residents to name basketball, so Plan A is biased no matter how many are asked. A smaller random sample of all residents represents the town better.

solve.answer: Plan B is better, because a random sample is more likely to represent the whole town
solve.work: Plan A samples only basketball spectators (biased); Plan B is random from the whole town, so more representative despite being smaller.

questions.skill: Taking an equal share from each group for a sample
questions.stem: A school has 200 sixth graders, 200 seventh graders and 200 eighth graders. Mia wants a sample of 60 students that includes the same number from each grade. How many students should she choose from each grade?
questions.solution: There are 3 grades and the sample must have the same number from each, so each grade gets $60 \div 3 = 20$ students.

questions.skill: Organizing data into a fraction of the whole
questions.stem: Twelve students recorded how many books they read last month: 2, 3, 3, 5, 0, 2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 5, 3. What fraction of the students read more than 3 books? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: The values greater than 3 are 5, 4 and 5, which is 3 students out of 12. The fraction is $\frac{3}{12} = \frac{1}{4}$.

solve.work: Values greater than 3: 5, 4, 5 = 3 students out of 12. 3/12 = 1/4.

questions.skill: Telling a statistical question from other questions
questions.stem: Four students each wrote a question about Ms. Chen's class. Which of these is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many minutes does it take each student in the class to walk to the gym?
How many hours a week do the students in the class play sports?
How many desks are in Ms. Chen's classroom?
How many pencils does each student in the class have in a desk?
questions.answer: How many desks are in Ms. Chen's classroom?
questions.solution: The number of desks in one classroom is a single fact with one answer, so it takes no data from a group. The other three questions have answers that differ from student to student, so each needs data from every student.

solve.answer: How many desks are in Ms. Chen's classroom?
solve.work: B, C, D ask about each student and vary. The number of desks in the room is one fixed count: not statistical.

questions.skill: Telling a statistical question from other questions
questions.stem: Sam wrote six questions. 1. How many brothers and sisters do the students in our class have? 2. How many brothers and sisters does Lena have? 3. What are the ages of the players on the town baseball team? 4. What are the weights of the pumpkins in the garden? 5. How long is each student's bus ride to school? 6. What day of the week is the school play? How many of the six questions are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Questions 1, 3, 4 and 5 ask about a whole group, and the answers will vary from one member to the next, so they are statistical. Question 2 is about one person and question 6 has one answer. That makes 4 statistical questions.

solve.work: 1 yes (siblings vary). 2 no (one person). 3 yes (ages vary). 4 yes (pumpkin weights vary). 5 yes (bus rides vary). 6 no (one day). Count = 4.

questions.skill: Choosing a statistical question that fits a situation
questions.stem: Mia wants to investigate one group of people: the sixth graders at Pine School. Which question is a statistical question about only that group?
choices: How many hours did Mia spend on homework last night?
How many hours a week do the sixth graders at Pine School and the adults in the town spend on homework?
What is the homework rule at Pine School?
How many hours a week do the sixth graders at Pine School spend on homework?
questions.answer: How many hours a week do the sixth graders at Pine School spend on homework?
questions.solution: The correct question asks about the sixth graders at Pine School and expects answers that vary. One option asks only about Mia, one adds a second group of people, and one asks about a rule, which has one answer.

solve.answer: How many hours a week do the sixth graders at Pine School spend on homework?
solve.work: A is a rule (one answer), B is Mia alone, D mixes two populations. C asks about the sixth graders at Pine School only, with varying answers.

questions.skill: Population and sample
questions.stem: A school has 900 students. The principal's sample is made up of 5% of the students. How many students are in the sample?
questions.solution: 5% of 900 is $0.05 \times 900 = 45$ students.

questions.skill: Population and sample
questions.stem: Which situation describes asking every member of the group instead of just a sample?
choices: A coach measures 5 of his team's 15 players to learn about his own team.
A coach measures all 15 players on his team to learn about every player in the league.
A coach measures 15 players from the league to learn about the 200 players in the league.
A coach measures all 15 players on his team to learn about his own team.
questions.answer: A coach measures all 15 players on his team to learn about his own team.
questions.solution: Asking everyone means measuring every member of the group you want to learn about. Only the coach who measures all 15 players on his team to learn about his own team measures the whole group of interest. In each of the others, the players measured are only part of the group the coach wants to know about.

solve.answer: A coach measures all 15 players on his team to learn about his own team.
solve.work: A census asks every member of the group being studied. B: all 15 players to learn about his own team. D measures all 15 but the group of interest is the league, so it is a sample. A and C are samples.

questions.skill: Population and sample
questions.stem: A school has 120 sixth graders, 120 seventh graders and 120 eighth graders. A sample has 15 students from each grade. What fraction of the school's students are in the sample? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: The school has $120 + 120 + 120 = 360$ students and the sample has $15 + 15 + 15 = 45$ students. The fraction is $\frac{45}{360} = \frac{1}{8}$.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased survey question
questions.stem: A survey asks, "How do you feel about the new bike lanes?" Which set of answer choices is balanced, with no push toward a good or a bad opinion?
choices: Love it, like it a lot, like it, dislike it
Like it, dislike it, dislike it a lot, hate it
Love it, like it a lot, like it, like it a little
Like a lot, like, dislike, dislike a lot
questions.answer: Like a lot, like, dislike, dislike a lot
questions.solution: A balanced set has as many positive choices as negative ones. "Like a lot, like, dislike, dislike a lot" has two of each. The other sets have three positive and one negative, or three negative and one positive, or only positive choices, which push people toward one kind of answer.

solve.answer: Like a lot, like, dislike, dislike a lot
solve.work: A: two positive, two negative, symmetric. B: 1 positive, 3 negative. C: 3 positive, 1 negative. D: all positive. Balanced = A.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative or random sample
questions.stem: A school numbers its 400 students from 1 to 400. A computer picks 25 different numbers from 1 to 400, and the students with those numbers are surveyed. Why is this a good way to choose a sample?
choices: Every student has the same chance of being chosen
It guarantees that every answer will be the same
It makes sure the oldest students are asked first
It makes sure exactly half of the sample are boys
questions.answer: Every student has the same chance of being chosen
questions.solution: Picking numbers at random gives every student the same chance of being chosen, which is what makes the sample fair. It does not control the students' answers, their ages or how many boys are chosen.

solve.answer: Every student has the same chance of being chosen
solve.work: Random selection by computer gives each of the 400 students the same chance of being chosen: B.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative or random sample
questions.stem: A town has $4{,}000$ residents: $1{,}000$ children and $3{,}000$ adults. A sample of 80 residents is chosen so that it matches the town's makeup. How many children are in the sample?
questions.solution: Children are $\frac{1{,}000}{4{,}000} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the residents, so they should be $\frac{1}{4}$ of the sample: $\frac{1}{4} \times 80 = 20$ children.

solve.work: Children are 1000/4000 = 1/4 of the town. 1/4 x 80 = 20.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative or random sample
questions.stem: A school has 240 sixth graders, 180 seventh graders and 180 eighth graders. A sample of 60 students is chosen to match the school. Which sample is correct?
choices: 20 sixth graders, 20 seventh graders, 20 eighth graders
30 sixth graders, 15 seventh graders, 15 eighth graders
18 sixth graders, 24 seventh graders, 18 eighth graders
24 sixth graders, 18 seventh graders, 18 eighth graders
questions.answer: 24 sixth graders, 18 seventh graders, 18 eighth graders
questions.solution: The school has $240 + 180 + 180 = 600$ students, and the sample is $\frac{60}{600} = \frac{1}{10}$ of them. One tenth of each grade is 24, 18 and 18 students.

solve.answer: 24 sixth graders, 18 seventh graders, 18 eighth graders

questions.skill: Sample size and the share of the population asked
questions.stem: A school has 480 students. The principal wants a sample of 5% of the students, and 8 students can be asked in each class period. How many class periods are needed?
questions.solution: 5% of 480 is $0.05 \times 480 = 24$ students. At 8 students per period, $24 \div 8 = 3$ class periods.

questions.skill: Organizing data in a frequency table
questions.stem: A frequency table shows how many glasses of water 40 students drank yesterday: 1 glass, 6 students; 2 glasses, 12 students; 3 glasses, a number not shown; 4 glasses, 7 students; 5 glasses, 2 students. How many glasses did the 40 students drink in all?
questions.solution: The missing number of students is $40 - 6 - 12 - 7 - 2 = 13$. Glasses in each row: $6 \times 1 = 6$, $12 \times 2 = 24$, $13 \times 3 = 39$, $7 \times 4 = 28$ and $2 \times 5 = 10$. The total is $6 + 24 + 39 + 28 + 10 = 107$ glasses.

questions.skill: Organizing data in a frequency table
questions.stem: A frequency table shows the ages of the 25 players in a league: age 10, 4 players; age 11, 8 players; age 12, 7 players; age 13, 6 players. How many more players are 11 or 12 years old than are 10 or 13 years old?
questions.solution: Players who are 11 or 12: $8 + 7 = 15$. Players who are 10 or 13: $4 + 6 = 10$. The difference is $15 - 10 = 5$ more players.

questions.skill: Organizing data in a frequency table
questions.stem: Fourteen students timed how many minutes they spent on a puzzle: 12, 25, 31, 18, 22, 9, 27, 35, 14, 20, 28, 33, 16, 24. Using the groups 0 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 29 and 30 to 39 minutes, how many students are in the group that has the most students?
questions.solution: Sort each time into its group: 0 to 9 has 1 student (9); 10 to 19 has 4 students (12, 18, 14, 16); 20 to 29 has 6 students (25, 22, 27, 20, 28, 24); 30 to 39 has 3 students (31, 35, 33). The largest group has 6 students.

questions.skill: Organizing survey results as fractions and percents
questions.stem: A survey of 60 students asked whether they want a later start time. Fifteen said yes, 33 said no and the rest were unsure. By how many percentage points is the percent of "no" answers greater than the percent of "yes" answers?
questions.solution: "No" is $\frac{33}{60} = 55\%$ and "yes" is $\frac{15}{60} = 25\%$. The difference is $55 - 25 = 30$ percentage points.

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: A class of 24 students answers the question "How many glasses of water do you drink each day?" Each student reports a number for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. How many numbers are in the whole data set?
questions.solution: Each of the 24 students gives 3 numbers, so there are $24 \times 3 = 72$ numbers.

questions.skill: Telling a statistical question from other questions
questions.stem: A nurse is gathering information about how much sleep middle school students get. Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: How many hours did Ravi sleep last night, according to what he told the nurse?
How many hours are in one day, counting the time spent asleep and the time awake?
How many hours of sleep did the nurse say that Ravi should get on school nights?
What is the typical number of hours that sixth graders sleep on a school night?
questions.answer: What is the typical number of hours that sixth graders sleep on a school night?
questions.solution: Different sixth graders sleep different numbers of hours, so answering takes data from many students, even though the answer asks for one "typical" number. The other questions each have one answer: one person's sleep on one night, the hours in a day, or a number the nurse already said.

solve.answer: What is the typical number of hours that sixth graders sleep on a school night?
solve.work: Typical sleep of sixth graders varies across students; the rest ask for one fixed fact.

questions.skill: Choosing a statistical question that fits a situation
questions.stem: The president of the chess club wants to learn about the ages of the club's members. Which question is a statistical question about exactly that group?
choices: What are the ages, in years, of the members of the school chess club?
How old is the club's president, who has been a member the longest?
How old are people who play chess in tournaments around the country?
What are the ages, in years, of all of the people who live in our town?
questions.answer: What are the ages, in years, of the members of the school chess club?
questions.solution: The question must name the club's members, and the ages will vary. The club's president is only one person, and the people who play chess in tournaments or who live in town are much larger groups than the club's members.

solve.answer: What are the ages, in years, of the members of the school chess club?
solve.work: Ages of the chess club members is statistical and about exactly that group; C and D are other populations, B is one person.

questions.skill: Choosing a statistical question that fits a situation
questions.stem: Noah's first question was "Did my friend Ben like the movie?" He now wants a statistical question about the sixth graders who saw the movie. Which question should he use?
choices: Did my friend Ben like the movie that we saw together on Saturday night?
How would the sixth graders who saw the movie rate it from 1 to 5?
How long is the movie that the sixth graders saw, in minutes?
What time does the movie start on Friday at the theater near school?
questions.answer: How would the sixth graders who saw the movie rate it from 1 to 5?
questions.solution: Ratings from many sixth graders will vary, so asking for them gives a statistical question about the right group. The other three questions are about one person or have one answer.

solve.answer: How would the sixth graders who saw the movie rate it from 1 to 5?
solve.work: Ratings from 1 to 5 by the sixth graders who saw the movie vary and concern that group.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased survey question
questions.stem: Which survey question is biased because it gives a reason for only one of the choices?
choices: Should the school add a gym class for all of the students, or keep the schedule the way it is now?
Which would you prefer for next year: a gym class, an art class, or no new class at all?
Should the school add a gym class, which would help students stay healthy, or keep the schedule as it is?
How many gym classes would you like each week, from zero classes up to three classes?
questions.answer: Should the school add a gym class, which would help students stay healthy, or keep the schedule as it is?
questions.solution: The correct option adds the reason "which would help students stay healthy" to the gym class only, which pushes people to choose it. The other three give no reason for either choice.

solve.answer: Should the school add a gym class, which would help students stay healthy, or keep the schedule as it is?
solve.work: Only A attaches a benefit (stay healthy) to one choice.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased survey question
questions.stem: Survey A asks, "How satisfied are you with the cafeteria's food?" Survey B asks, "How satisfied are you with the cafeteria's food, which is made fresh each day?" Which statement is true?
choices: Survey B is biased because it adds a fact that pushes people toward a high rating
Survey A is biased because it uses the word satisfied, which pushes people toward a high rating
Both surveys are biased because they ask people to rate food, an opinion
Neither survey is biased because both ask about the same cafeteria
questions.answer: Survey B is biased because it adds a fact that pushes people toward a high rating
questions.solution: Survey A simply asks how satisfied people are. Survey B adds "which is made fresh each day," a good thing that nudges people to rate the food higher. That makes only Survey B biased.

solve.answer: Survey B is biased because it adds a fact that pushes people toward a high rating
solve.work: B adds a positive fact (made fresh daily) that nudges toward higher ratings; A is neutral.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased way of choosing a sample
questions.stem: Raj wants to estimate how many miles a week people in his town run. He asks 100 people who just finished a running race. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: His estimate will probably be too high, because people at a race run more than most people
His estimate will probably be too low, because people who just finished a race are tired
His estimate will be accurate, because 100 people is a large enough sample to be reliable
His estimate will be accurate, because every one of the people he asked ran at least some miles
questions.answer: His estimate will probably be too high, because people at a race run more than most people
questions.solution: People who just finished a race are runners, who run more than most people in town. The sample is not typical of the town, so his estimate would be too high, no matter how many runners he asks.

solve.answer: His estimate will probably be too high, because people at a race run more than most people
solve.work: Race finishers run more than typical residents, so the estimate is likely too high.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased way of choosing a sample
questions.stem: A phone survey calls homes at 2 p.m. on weekdays to learn how many hours adults in a town work each week. Why might the sample be biased?
choices: Phone calls cost too much money, so the survey cannot reach enough homes in the town
Adults who work during the day are less likely to be home at that time to answer
Adults do not know how many hours they work, so they cannot answer the question
The survey calls far too many homes, so the answers will be too hard to put together
questions.answer: Adults who work during the day are less likely to be home at that time to answer
questions.solution: At 2 p.m. on a weekday, adults with jobs are at work, so the people who answer are mostly adults who work fewer hours or do not work. Their answers would not match all the adults in town.

solve.answer: Adults who work during the day are less likely to be home at that time to answer
solve.work: Weekday 2 p.m. calls miss adults working daytime hours, under-representing workers.

questions.skill: Spotting a biased way of choosing a sample
questions.stem: Ben wants to know the favorite game of all 500 students at his school. He asks his 12 friends. Which statement describes the main problem?
choices: Friends tend to like the same things, so his friends may not represent all the students
He should have asked exactly half of the students, so that the sample matches the population
His friends will always say what they think he wants to hear, so none of their answers are true
Favorite games cannot be studied with a survey, because favorites change from one day to the next
questions.answer: Friends tend to like the same things, so his friends may not represent all the students
questions.solution: Ben picked the people who were easiest to ask, and friends often have similar interests. His 12 friends might not match the 500 students. A sample does not have to be half of the population.

solve.answer: Friends tend to like the same things, so his friends may not represent all the students
solve.work: Friends share interests, so 12 friends may not represent all 500 students.

questions.skill: Sample size and the share of the population asked
questions.stem: Which statement about samples is true?
choices: A larger sample always removes bias, because more people match the whole population better
A sample must be as large as the whole population to give a useful picture of what everyone thinks
A larger, random sample usually gives a better picture, but one large biased sample is still biased
A random sample of 5 is just as reliable as a random sample of 500, as long as both are chosen fairly
questions.answer: A larger, random sample usually gives a better picture, but one large biased sample is still biased
questions.solution: More members in a random sample usually means a closer match to the population. But a large sample can still be biased if it is chosen unfairly. A sample does not have to be as big as the population, and a tiny sample is less reliable than a large one.

solve.answer: A larger, random sample usually gives a better picture, but one large biased sample is still biased
solve.work: Larger random samples usually help but size does not fix bias; A, B, C are false.

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: A class wants to answer the question "How many hours a day do the students in our class spend outdoors?" Which plan collects the right data?
choices: Ask each student whether they like being outdoors, with the answer yes or no
Ask each student for the hours spent outdoors on each day of one week
Ask each student for the name of a favorite outdoor game to play at recess
Ask only one student for the hours spent outdoors on Monday
questions.answer: Ask each student for the hours spent outdoors on each day of one week
questions.solution: The question is about hours per day for the students in the class, so the plan must collect hours from every student. Whether they like it, a favorite game, or one student's Monday do not give that data.

solve.answer: Ask each student for the hours spent outdoors on each day of one week
solve.issues: Soft: the keyed plan collects hours per day for a week, which answers 'hours a day'; fine, though 'a typical day' is implied rather than stated.
solve.work: Hours outdoors per day for each student over a week gives the data on hours a day; A is one student, C/D are not hours.

questions.skill: Deciding what data to collect and record
questions.stem: A teacher wants to answer "How long do the students in the school take to eat lunch?" Which is the best way to record the data?
choices: Record the number of minutes each student takes, to the nearest minute
Record fast or slow for each student, depending on how long lunch takes
Record the time of day when each student finishes eating, such as 12:15
Record how many students eat lunch in the cafeteria on each day of the week
questions.answer: Record the number of minutes each student takes, to the nearest minute
questions.solution: The question asks about a length of time, so the best record is the number of minutes for each student. Fast or slow is not precise, the finishing time is a time of day rather than a length, and the number of students does not measure time.

solve.answer: Record the number of minutes each student takes, to the nearest minute
solve.work: Duration in minutes per student answers how long; finishing time alone is not duration, fast/slow loses detail.

questions.skill: Choosing a representative sample
questions.stem: A town has 5,000 residents. To answer "How many hours a week do residents spend outdoors?", three plans are made. Plan A mails the question to 50 residents chosen at random. Plan B asks the 50 people shopping in a hiking store. Plan C posts the question on the town website, where 90 residents choose to answer. Which plan is most likely to represent all the residents?
choices: Plan A, because the residents were chosen at random
Plan B, because all 50 people answered at once
Plan C, because it has the most answers
All three plans are equally likely to represent the residents
questions.answer: Plan A, because the residents were chosen at random
questions.solution: A random choice gives every resident a chance to be asked, so the sample is likely to represent the town. People in a hiking store probably spend more time outdoors than most residents, and people who volunteer on a website may differ from the rest. More answers do not fix that kind of bias.

solve.answer: Plan A, because the residents were chosen at random
solve.work: Random selection gives a representative sample; B is biased toward hikers, C is voluntary response.

questions.skill: Samples and populations
questions.stem: A researcher wants to answer "How many hours a week do sixth graders in North Carolina spend reading?" She decides to ask a random sample instead of every sixth grader. Which reason is correct?
choices: Asking every sixth grader would cost too much time and money, and a random sample can still represent them
A sample always gives exactly the same answer as asking every single sixth grader in the whole state
Only answers from a sample can ever be biased, while answers from every student never can be
A sample of the students who are easiest to reach is a better choice than a random sample
questions.answer: Asking every sixth grader would cost too much time and money, and a random sample can still represent them
questions.solution: A well-chosen random sample is much cheaper and quicker, and it is likely to look like the whole group. It does not give exactly the same answer, and a badly worded question can bias the answers of everyone. A random sample is better than only the easiest students to reach.

solve.answer: Asking every sixth grader would cost too much time and money, and a random sample can still represent them
solve.work: A census of the state is costly; a random sample can represent the population. Other options are false.

questions.skill: Representative samples in proportion
questions.stem: A school has 240 sixth graders, 360 seventh graders and 400 eighth graders. A sample of 50 students is chosen so that each grade is in the sample in the same proportion as in the school. How many seventh graders are in the sample?
questions.solution: The school has $240 + 360 + 400 = 1000$ students, and seventh graders are $\frac{360}{1000}$ of them. The sample should have the same share: $\frac{360}{1000} \times 50 = 18$ seventh graders.

questions.skill: Reading the total from a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows the number of pets owned by students, with one dot for each student. It has these dots: 0 pets, 3 dots; 1 pet, 5 dots; 2 pets, 4 dots; 3 pets, 2 dots. How many students are shown on the dot plot?
questions.solution: Each dot is one student, so add the dots: $3 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 14$ students.

questions.skill: Finding the tallest bar of a histogram
questions.stem: A histogram of 16 quiz scores has bars with these heights: 0 to 9, 2 scores; 10 to 19, 6 scores; 20 to 29, 5 scores; 30 to 39, 3 scores. Which interval contains the most scores?
questions.solution: The tallest bar is the one with the greatest height. The interval 10 to 19 has 6 scores, which is more than any other interval.

solve.work: Heights 2, 6, 5, 3 (total 16). Tallest bar is 10 to 19 with 6.

questions.skill: Range from the five key values of a box plot
questions.stem: A box plot of daily visitors to a park has a minimum of 12, a first quartile of 20, a median of 26, a third quartile of 34 and a maximum of 50. What is the range of the data?
questions.solution: The range is the maximum minus the minimum: $50 - 12 = 38$. (14 is the IQR, $34 - 20$; 26 is the median.)

questions.skill: Reading counts and totals from a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows how many books each of 12 students read in March, with one dot for each student. The stacks of dots are: 1 book, 2 dots; 2 books, 5 dots; 3 books, 4 dots; 4 books, 1 dot. How many students read exactly 2 books?
questions.solution: Find the stack above 2 books. It has 5 dots, and each dot is one student, so 5 students read exactly 2 books.

solve.work: The stack above 2 books has 5 dots. Check total: 2+5+4+1 = 12.

questions.skill: Reading counts and totals from a dot plot
questions.stem: On a dot plot of the number of siblings each student has, the tallest stack of dots is above the number 2. What does that tell you?
choices: More students have 2 siblings than any other number of siblings
The greatest number of siblings any student has is 2
questions.answer: More students have 2 siblings than any other number of siblings
questions.solution: A taller stack means more dots, and each dot is one student. So the tallest stack shows the number of siblings that the most students have. It does not say that everyone has 2 siblings, or that 2 is the greatest number.

solve.answer: More students have 2 siblings than any other number of siblings
solve.work: Each dot is one student; the tallest stack is the most common value, so more students have 2 siblings than any other number. It says nothing about how many were asked, the maximum, or everyone.

questions.skill: Reading counts and totals from a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows the number of goals a soccer team scored in each of its games. What does each dot on the plot stand for?
questions.solution: The data are one number of goals for each game, so every dot stands for one game. The number line under the dots tells how many goals were scored in that game.

solve.work: The plot records goals per game, so each dot is one game placed above its number of goals.

questions.skill: Clusters, gaps, peaks and outliers in a dot plot
questions.stem: Which statement best describes an outlier in a dot plot?
choices: The value that has the most dots
The value in the middle of the data
The largest value in the data
A value that is far away from most of the other values
questions.answer: A value that is far away from most of the other values
questions.solution: An outlier sits far from the rest of the data. The value with the most dots is the peak, the value in the middle is the median, and the largest value is only an outlier if it is far from the others.

solve.answer: A value that is far away from most of the other values
solve.work: An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. The largest value need not be an outlier; middle is the median; most dots is the mode.

questions.skill: Clusters, gaps, peaks and outliers in a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot of shoe sizes has these stacks of dots: size 5, 1 dot; size 6, 3 dots; size 7, 4 dots; size 10, 2 dots. There are no dots at sizes 8 and 9. Where is the gap in the plot?
choices: At size 7, where the stack is tallest
At size 5, where the stack is shortest
At sizes 8 and 9, where there are no dots
questions.answer: At sizes 8 and 9, where there are no dots
questions.solution: A gap is a stretch of the number line with no dots. Sizes 8 and 9 have none, so that is the gap. The tallest and shortest stacks have dots, so they are not gaps.

solve.answer: At sizes 8 and 9, where there are no dots
solve.work: A gap is an interval with no data: sizes 8 and 9.

questions.skill: Clusters, gaps, peaks and outliers in a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows these 9 values, with one dot for each value: 12, 13, 13, 14, 14, 14, 15, 15, 30. Which value is an outlier?
questions.solution: Eight of the values are between 12 and 15, close together. The value 30 is far from all of them, so 30 is the outlier.

solve.work: Values cluster from 12 to 15; 30 is far from all others, so 30 is the outlier.

questions.skill: Constructing a dot plot from a list of data
questions.stem: Ana lists the number of goals her team scored in 10 games: 2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1. She makes a dot plot with one dot for each game. How many dots go above the number 2?
questions.solution: Count how many times 2 appears in the list: it is the 1st, 4th, 6th and 9th number. That is 4 games, so 4 dots go above 2.

solve.work: Values equal to 2: 2,0,1,2,3,2,1,0,2,1 -> positions 1,4,6,9 = 4 dots stacked above 2. (Counts: 0:2, 1:3, 2:4, 3:1 = 10.)

questions.skill: Constructing a dot plot from a list of data
questions.stem: Raj measured the heights of his plants. The heights run from 12 cm to 20 cm, and each one is a whole number of centimeters. He will make a dot plot. Which number line is the best choice?
choices: Marks from 0 to 100, with one mark for every 20 centimeters
Marks from 12 to 20, with one mark for every 4 centimeters
Marks from 12 to 20, with one mark for each centimeter
Marks from 0 to 12, with one mark for each centimeter
questions.answer: Marks from 12 to 20, with one mark for each centimeter
questions.solution: The number line must cover every height from 12 to 20 and have a mark for each whole centimeter, so that every plant gets its own place. The other lines are too coarse to show each height, or they do not reach the tallest plants.

solve.answer: Marks from 12 to 20, with one mark for each centimeter
solve.work: Whole-cm data from 12 to 20 need marks covering 12-20 at every centimeter. Every 4 cm cannot place 13, 14, etc.; 0-12 misses data; 0-100 by 20s is too coarse.

questions.skill: Reading bar heights and totals in a histogram
questions.stem: A histogram shows how many minutes 30 students read last night. The bars are: 0 to 9 minutes, 4 students; 10 to 19 minutes, 11 students; 20 to 29 minutes, 9 students; 30 to 39 minutes, 6 students. How many students read for 20 to 29 minutes?
questions.solution: The height of the bar for 20 to 29 minutes is 9, so 9 students read for 20 to 29 minutes.

solve.work: The 20-29 bar holds 9 students. Total 4+11+9+6 = 30 checks.

questions.skill: Reading bar heights and totals in a histogram
questions.stem: In a histogram, what does the height of a bar show?
choices: How many values are in that bar's interval
The most common value in the interval
The total of all the values in the interval
questions.answer: How many values are in that bar's interval
questions.solution: Each bar covers an interval of values, and its height counts how many data values fall in that interval. It does not show the most common value, the width of the interval, or the total of the values.

solve.answer: How many values are in that bar's interval
solve.work: A histogram bar height is the frequency: how many values fall in that interval.

questions.skill: Reading bar heights and totals in a histogram
questions.stem: A histogram of the ages of people at a library has these bars: 0 to 4 years, 7 people; 5 to 9 years, 12 people; 10 to 14 years, 9 people; 15 to 19 years, 4 people. How many people are in the data set?
questions.solution: Every person is counted in exactly one bar, so add the bars: $7 + 12 + 9 + 4 = 32$ people.

questions.skill: Placing values in histogram intervals
questions.stem: A histogram of the minutes students spend on homework uses the intervals 0 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 29 and 30 to 39. In which interval is a time of 20 minutes counted?
questions.solution: The interval 20 to 29 starts at 20, so a time of exactly 20 minutes goes in that bar. The interval 10 to 19 stops at 19.

questions.skill: Placing values in histogram intervals
questions.stem: Dan's data are 3, 7, 12, 8, 15, 4, 9, 11. He makes a histogram with the intervals 0 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14 and 15 to 19. How many values are in the interval 5 to 9?
questions.solution: The values from 5 to 9 are 7, 8 and 9. That is 3 values.

questions.skill: Placing values in histogram intervals
questions.stem: Which set of intervals is best for a histogram of ages from 0 to 49, with equal widths and no gaps or overlaps?
questions.solution: Good intervals have the same width, start where the last one stopped and do not overlap. The intervals 0 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 29, 30 to 39 and 40 to 49 each hold 10 whole numbers and fit together. Intervals such as 0 to 10 and 10 to 20 overlap at 10. An interval of 20 to 39 is wider than the others. Intervals 0 to 9, 20 to 29 and 40 to 49 leave gaps.

solve.work: Option 4: five intervals of width 10, covering 0-49 with no gap or overlap. Option 1 overlaps at 10, 20, ... and runs to 50; option 2 has unequal width (20-39); option 3 has gaps.

questions.skill: Describing the shape and spread of a histogram
questions.stem: A histogram has five bars. Their heights, from left to right, are 2, 5, 6, 5 and 2. Which word best describes its shape?
choices: Skewed to the right (a long tail toward larger values)
Skewed to the left (a long tail toward smaller values)
Symmetric, with the peak in the middle
Flat, with all the bars the same height
questions.answer: Symmetric, with the peak in the middle
questions.solution: The bars rise to the tallest one in the middle and fall the same way on the other side, so the left and right halves mirror each other. That is a symmetric shape.

solve.answer: Symmetric, with the peak in the middle
solve.work: 2,5,6,5,2 mirrors about the middle bar: symmetric with the peak in the middle.

questions.skill: Describing the shape and spread of a histogram
questions.stem: The tallest bar of a histogram is on the far left, and the bars get steadily shorter toward the right. What is its shape?
choices: Skewed to the left, with a long tail toward smaller values
Symmetric, with the peak in the middle
Flat, with all the bars the same height
Skewed to the right, with a long tail toward larger values
questions.answer: Skewed to the right, with a long tail toward larger values
questions.solution: Most of the values are small, and fewer and fewer values are larger. The tail of the histogram stretches to the right, toward larger values, so it is skewed to the right.

solve.answer: Skewed to the right, with a long tail toward larger values
solve.work: Peak on the left, bars tailing off to the right: long tail toward larger values = skewed right.

questions.skill: Finding the median from a display
questions.stem: A dot plot of the number of pages in five books has one dot at each of 120, 140, 150, 180 and 200 pages. What is the median number of pages?
questions.solution: The values are already in order. With 5 values, the median is the middle one, the 3rd: 150 pages.

questions.skill: Finding the median from a display
questions.stem: A dot plot of the number of pets owned by 9 students has these stacks of dots: 1 pet, 3 dots; 2 pets, 5 dots; 3 pets, 1 dot. What is the median number of pets?
questions.solution: List the 9 values in order: 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3. The median is the 5th value, which is 2 pets.

questions.skill: Finding the five key values of a data set
questions.stem: Kai records the number of push-ups he does on five days: 14, 9, 12, 20, 11. What is the median?
questions.solution: Put the numbers in order: 9, 11, 12, 14, 20. The middle one, the 3rd, is 12.

questions.skill: Finding the five key values of a data set
questions.stem: Which list gives the five key values of a box plot in order from least to greatest?
choices: Minimum, median, first quartile, third quartile, maximum
Minimum, first quartile, third quartile, median, maximum
Minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum
First quartile, minimum, median, maximum, third quartile
questions.answer: Minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum
questions.solution: The minimum is the least value and the maximum is the greatest. In between come the first quartile, the median and the third quartile, in that order, because the median is in the middle of the data.

solve.answer: Minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum
solve.work: Five-number summary in order: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.

questions.skill: Finding the five key values of a data set
questions.stem: The 8 ordered values of a data set are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. The median is 9. What is the median of the lower half of the data, which is the first quartile?
questions.solution: The lower half is the first 4 values: 2, 4, 6, 8. Its median is halfway between 4 and 6, which is $(4 + 6) \div 2 = 5$.

questions.skill: Reading range and IQR from a box plot
questions.stem: In a box plot of the heights of sunflowers, in centimeters, the left whisker starts at 100. The box runs from 140 to 170, with the median line at 152, and the right whisker ends at 182. How long is the right whisker, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The right whisker runs from the right end of the box, 170, to its end, 182. Its length is $182 - 170 = 12$ centimeters.

solve.work: Right whisker runs from Q3 = 170 to max 182: 12 cm.

questions.skill: Reading range and IQR from a box plot
questions.stem: What part of the data does the box of a box plot cover?
choices: All of the values, from the minimum to the maximum
The middle half of the values, from the first quartile to the third quartile
The lower half of the values, up to the median
Only the values that are equal to the median
questions.answer: The middle half of the values, from the first quartile to the third quartile
questions.solution: The box stretches from the first quartile to the third quartile, and the median line is inside it. About one half of the values lie in the box. The whiskers cover the rest, out to the minimum and maximum.

solve.answer: The middle half of the values, from the first quartile to the third quartile
solve.work: The box spans Q1 to Q3: the middle half of the data.

questions.skill: Reading range and IQR from a box plot
questions.stem: A box plot shows the minutes that students spend on homework. The box starts at 20 and ends at 45. What is the interquartile range, in minutes?
questions.solution: The IQR is the length of the box: third quartile minus first quartile. That is $45 - 20 = 25$ minutes.

questions.skill: Share of the data in a part of a box plot
questions.stem: About what fraction of the values in a data set lie between the first quartile and the third quartile?
questions.solution: The quartiles split the ordered data into four parts with about the same number of values. The box covers the two middle parts, from the first quartile to the third quartile, so it holds about one half of the values.

solve.work: Q1 to Q3 holds the middle half of the data.

questions.skill: Comparing the center and spread of two displays
questions.stem: Class A's box plot of test scores has a median of 70. Class B's box plot has a median of 80. What does this tell you?
choices: The typical score in Class B is higher than in Class A
Every student in Class B scored higher than every student in Class A
Class B's scores are more spread out than Class A's
Class A has more students than Class B
questions.answer: The typical score in Class B is higher than in Class A
questions.solution: The median is a measure of the center, or the typical value. A higher median means a higher typical score. It does not say that every student scored higher, how spread out the scores are, or how many students there are.

solve.answer: The typical score in Class B is higher than in Class A
solve.work: Median measures a typical value: B (80) is typically higher than A (70). It says nothing about spread, class size, or every student.

questions.skill: Reading displays with unusual scales or layouts
questions.stem: A line plot of the lengths of pencil stubs, in inches, has these stacks of dots: $\frac{1}{2}$ inch, 2 dots; $\frac{3}{4}$ inch, 4 dots; 1 inch, 3 dots. Which length is the most common?
questions.solution: The tallest stack is above $\frac{3}{4}$ inch, with 4 dots, so $\frac{3}{4}$ inch is the most common length. The stack at $\frac{1}{2}$ inch has 2 dots and the stack at 1 inch has 3. There are no dots at $\frac{1}{4}$ inch.

solve.work: 3/4 inch has the tallest stack (4 dots).

questions.skill: Choosing a display and knowing what it shows
questions.stem: Mira has the number of siblings of 12 students. She wants a display that shows every single value as its own dot. Which display should she make?
questions.solution: A dot plot puts one dot above the number line for each value, so every value is shown. A histogram groups values into bars, and a box plot shows only five key values.

solve.work: A dot plot shows each value as its own dot; box plots and histograms summarise, circle graphs show parts of a whole.

questions.skill: Choosing a display and knowing what it shows
questions.stem: Which question can a box plot answer directly?
choices: How many values are in the data set?
questions.solution: The line inside the box marks the median. A box plot shows only five key values, so it cannot tell how many values there are, how many equal a given number, or which value occurs most often.

solve.work: A box plot shows the five-number summary, so it gives the median directly; it does not show the count, exact frequencies or the mode.

questions.skill: Choosing a display and knowing what it shows
questions.stem: Which display groups data into equal intervals and uses the height of each bar to show how many values are in an interval?
questions.solution: A histogram has one bar for each interval, and the height of the bar is the number of values in that interval. A dot plot shows each value as a dot and a box plot shows five key values.

solve.work: Equal intervals with bar heights for counts: a histogram.

questions.skill: Interquartile range from five key values
questions.stem: Forty students recorded how many minutes they read. The smallest time was 4, the first quartile was 9, the median was 15, the third quartile was 22 and the largest time was 31. What is the interquartile range (IQR) in minutes?
questions.solution: The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first quartile: $22 - 9 = 13$ minutes.

questions.skill: Describing a gap and an outlier in a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows the number of goals scored in 19 games: 0 goals, 4 dots; 1 goal, 6 dots; 2 goals, 5 dots; 3 goals, 3 dots; 4 goals, 0 dots; 5 goals, 0 dots; 6 goals, 1 dot. Which statement is true?
choices: The most common number of goals was 6
There is a gap between 3 and 6, and the value 6 is far from the rest of the data
Every number of goals from 0 to 6 occurred at least once
Most games had 4 or more goals
questions.answer: There is a gap between 3 and 6, and the value 6 is far from the rest of the data
questions.solution: No game had 4 or 5 goals, so there is a gap between 3 and 6. Only one game had 6 goals, far from the others. The most common number was 1 goal (6 games), and 4 or more goals happened in only 1 game.

solve.answer: There is a gap between 3 and 6, and the value 6 is far from the rest of the data
solve.work: Total 4+6+5+3+0+0+1 = 19. Games with 4+ goals: 1 (not most). Mode is 1 goal, not 6. 4 and 5 goals never occurred. So there is a gap (4, 5) between 3 and 6, and 6 is an outlier.

questions.skill: Finding the interval that holds the median of a histogram
questions.stem: A histogram of 19 ages has these bars: 1 to 5, 6 values; 6 to 10, 5 values; 11 to 15, 4 values; 16 to 20, 4 values. In which interval is the median age?
questions.solution: With 19 values, the median is the 10th value in order. The first bar holds values 1 to 6, and the second bar holds values 7 to 11. So the 10th value is in the interval 6 to 10.

solve.work: 19 values (6+5+4+4), median is the 10th. Values 1-6 are in 1 to 5; values 7-11 are in 6 to 10. The 10th lies in 6 to 10.

questions.skill: Reading counts and totals from a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows the number of minutes that 20 students took to finish a puzzle. The stacks of dots are: 5 minutes, 3 dots; 10 minutes, 6 dots; 15 minutes, 5 dots; 20 minutes, 4 dots; 25 minutes, 2 dots. How many students took more than 10 minutes?
questions.solution: "More than 10 minutes" means the stacks at 15, 20 and 25 minutes. Add their dots: $5 + 4 + 2 = 11$ students.

questions.skill: Reading counts and totals from a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot of 15 quiz scores has these stacks of dots: score 6, 2 dots; score 7, 3 dots; score 8, 5 dots; score 9, 3 dots; score 10, 2 dots. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: The stack above 8 has 5 dots, so 5 students scored 8. The stack above 10 has only 2 dots, no one scored 5, and 15 is the total number of students, not the number who scored 8.

solve.work: Stack above 8 has 5 dots: five students scored 8. Score 10 has 2 dots; 5 is not a score; total 2+3+5+3+2 = 15.

questions.skill: Clusters, gaps, peaks and outliers in a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows the time, in minutes, that 15 students take to walk to school. The stacks of dots are: 5 minutes, 2 dots; 6 minutes, 3 dots; 7 minutes, 5 dots; 8 minutes, 4 dots; 25 minutes, 1 dot. There are no other dots. Which statement describes the plot?
choices: The times are spread evenly from 5 to 25 minutes
The peak of the plot is at 25 minutes
The times form one cluster from 5 to 25 minutes with no gaps
Most times are clustered from 5 to 8 minutes, with an outlier at 25 minutes
questions.answer: Most times are clustered from 5 to 8 minutes, with an outlier at 25 minutes
questions.solution: Fourteen of the 15 dots are between 5 and 8 minutes, so that is the cluster, and the peak is at 7 minutes. The dot at 25 minutes is far from the others, so it is an outlier, and there is a gap between 8 and 25.

solve.answer: Most times are clustered from 5 to 8 minutes, with an outlier at 25 minutes
solve.work: Total 2+3+5+4+1 = 15. Dots fill 5 to 8, then a gap until a single dot at 25: a cluster 5-8 with an outlier at 25. Peak is at 7, not 25; not even, not gap-free.

questions.skill: Clusters, gaps, peaks and outliers in a dot plot
questions.stem: A dot plot shows the ages of the people at a chess club: 11 years, 3 dots; 12 years, 5 dots; 13 years, 4 dots; 14 years, 2 dots; 40 years, 1 dot. The dot at 40 years is the coach. What is the range of the students' ages, not counting the coach?
questions.solution: Without the coach, the youngest student is 11 and the oldest is 14. The range is $14 - 11 = 3$ years.

questions.skill: Constructing a dot plot from a list of data
questions.stem: Mia counts the pencils in 10 backpacks and lists the numbers: 3, 5, 4, 3, 5, 5, 6, 4, 3, 5. She makes a dot plot with one dot for each backpack. Which description of her dot plot is correct?
choices: 3 pencils, 3 dots; 4 pencils, 3 dots; 5 pencils, 3 dots; 6 pencils, 1 dot
3 pencils, 3 dots; 4 pencils, 2 dots; 5 pencils, 4 dots; 6 pencils, 1 dot
3 pencils, 2 dots; 4 pencils, 2 dots; 5 pencils, 4 dots; 6 pencils, 1 dot
3 pencils, 4 dots; 4 pencils, 2 dots; 5 pencils, 3 dots; 6 pencils, 1 dot
questions.answer: 3 pencils, 3 dots; 4 pencils, 2 dots; 5 pencils, 4 dots; 6 pencils, 1 dot
questions.solution: Count each number in the list: 3 appears 3 times, 4 appears 2 times, 5 appears 4 times and 6 appears once. That is $3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 10$ dots, one for each backpack.

solve.answer: 3 pencils, 3 dots; 4 pencils, 2 dots; 5 pencils, 4 dots; 6 pencils, 1 dot
solve.work: 3s: positions 1,4,9 = 3. 4s: positions 3,8 = 2. 5s: positions 2,5,6,10 = 4. 6: 1. Total 10. Matches option 1.

questions.skill: Constructing a dot plot from a list of data
questions.stem: The heights of 15 plants run from 12 cm to 20 cm, and each is a whole number of centimeters. Raj makes a number line for a dot plot with a mark for every whole centimeter from the shortest height to the tallest height, including both. How many marks does he draw?
questions.solution: The marks are 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 20. Count both ends: $20 - 12 + 1 = 9$ marks.

questions.skill: Reading bar heights and totals in a histogram
questions.stem: A histogram of the weights of 28 backpacks has these bars: 0 to 4 pounds, 3 backpacks; 5 to 9 pounds, 8 backpacks; 10 to 14 pounds, 12 backpacks; 15 to 19 pounds, 5 backpacks. How many backpacks weigh 10 pounds or more?
questions.solution: Backpacks that weigh 10 pounds or more are in the bars for 10 to 14 and 15 to 19. Add them: $12 + 5 = 17$ backpacks.
